title: C64PrgLoader entry/degrade-path regressions from arbitrary load-address rework
description:
From /code-review of codex commit fd17727 (grm-dvx arbitrary PRG load addresses). Five related regressions vs the old fixed-0x0801 loader, all in src/main/java/retromachines/C64PrgLoader.java:

1. ENTRY POINT SILENTLY DROPPED (CONFIRMED, ~line 409): entry creation is gated on entryBlock.isExecute(); a load address landing in a non-executable block (P6510 io-kind at $0000, canExecute=false) gets a label but no external entry point, no function, and no log message. Old loader added them unconditionally. Repro: full-memory-snapshot PRG with load address $0000.

2. 2-BYTE HEADER-ONLY PRG REJECTED (CONFIRMED, ~line 210): findSupportedLoadSpecs minimum went 2 -> 3, so a zero-payload .prg falls through to the raw Binary loader instead of importing with the full C64 map/symbols as before; also makes the prgLength==0 IOException (~272) dead code.

3. STRUCT ACROSS CARVED BOUNDARY (PLAUSIBLE, ~line 556): createCarvedTarget applies the region struct (2-byte R6510) at the region start even when slices split the region into initialized+uninitialized blocks; createData fails (only logged), 6510 port registers left untyped. Repro with shipped map: load $FF00, 0x101 payload (wrap covers only $0000).

4. DEGRADE PATH ABORTS (PLAUSIBLE, ~line 644): when banked-window setup is skipped ('skipping banked-window setup'), window-occupant slices never get a placement space and persistPrgPlacement throws 'No address space was created for PRG target RAM_A000', aborting the import the skip message promised to survive. Sibling: planPrgSlices (~494) NPEs on a map with no windows array — a shape load() explicitly supports. Both need hand-edited/variant maps today (MapCompiler always emits the keys) but the loader's own code claims to support the shapes.

5. PLACEMENT GAPS ABORT IMPORT, NO VALIDATOR (PLAUSIBLE, ~line 532): != 1 placement targets per PRG byte now throws instead of the old log-and-single-block degrade. Shipped c64.yaml is gapless today, but nothing (MapCompiler or CI) validates coverage, so the first map edit that opens a gap breaks every spanning PRG import.

Suggested split if needed: 1+2 are quick behavioral fixes; 3 needs applyStructType to skip/split when the region is carved; 4 wants either upfront validation with a clear error or a real degrade; 5 wants a MapCompiler coverage check.
acceptance_criteria: PRG at $0000 gets an entry point (or an explicit log explaining the drop); 2-byte PRG imports with C64 map again or the rejection is deliberate+documented; wrapped $FF00 import leaves R6510 typed; skipped-window and gap cases either import degraded or fail with a clear validation error, covered by banktest fixtures.
notes: Item #3 (struct across carved boundary) was PLAUSIBLE and does NOT reproduce in Ghidra 12.1.2 -- verified empirically in grm-z15.2 (fixture prgstraddletest): createData spans an init/uninit block boundary fine, so R6510 types correctly at $0000-$0001. Resolved as a guarded non-bug, no code change.
close_reason: All five reviewed regressions resolved across sub-beads z15.1-z15.4: #1 entry point restored (unconditional external entry + gated function mark + log), #2 2-byte PRG accepted again, #3 verified NOT reproducible in 12.1.2 (createData spans a carved block boundary; kept a guard fixture), #4 degrade path made honest (windows NPE guard + up-front clear error), #5 compile-time placement coverage check + declarative prg_placeable flag. Follow-ups: grm-abg (malformed-map harness for #4 runtime coverage), C128 P8502 prg_placeable. Full gate green throughout.

title: AnalyzerRunLog lifecycle: markCompleted fires on failure paths and before the phase-2 follow-on round
description:
From /code-review of codex commits 065577e..fd17727 (commit 837148d, grm-olp quieting). Two confirmed defects in when AnalyzerRunLog.markCompleted is called:

1. FAILURE PATHS CONSUME THE ONE-SHOT VERBOSITY: BoardBankAnalyzer.added() calls markCompleted on the map-load IOException path (~line 228), BoardModel.parse null (~234), and empty-mechanisms (~244); C64BasicAnalyzer does the same on gdt/petscii open failures (~175/185). A transient first-run failure permanently silences the first *successful* run (no 'running', no helper list, no summary) — and AnalyzerRunLog has no reset API.

2. MARKED BEFORE THE FOLLOW-ON FULL ROUND: markCompleted fires at the end of round 1 (~line 337), but the adjacent LAST_COMPLETED comment documents that phase-2 disassembly side effects deliberately trigger a framework re-run 'in full'. That completing round of the same initial analysis runs verbose=false, so the only summary ever logged carries stale round-1 counts.

Fix direction: mark completed only after a successful, fixpoint-reached run (e.g. move the body into doAdded() and mark at the single wrapper exit only when the run did real work and the LAST_COMPLETED fingerprint matches), and consider an AnalyzerRunLog reset when analysis config changes. Also note markCompleted call sites are copy-pasted on ~9 exit paths across the two analyzers — a structural wrapper removes the whole class of miss.
acceptance_criteria: First successful analysis after a failed run logs verbosely; the summary logged reflects the final (fixpoint) round's counts; regression covered by a banktest fixture or unit check.
notes: Implementation staged 2026-07-18: AnalyzerRunLog uses a v2 persisted key so saved Programs polluted by the old failure policy get one clean retry; C64BasicAnalyzer centralizes completion so false/exception/cancellation paths remain initial while successful work/no-ops complete; BoardBankAnalyzer defers summary, cache stamp, and completion until entry/exit function+instruction fingerprints are stable, and no longer completes descriptor/resource/strategy failure paths. Regression additions cover legacy-key migration, failure followed by verbose successful BASIC retry, real banking v2 completion, and the fixpoint predicate. Validation completed: production compileJava PASS; VerifyBankTest.java standalone compilation against Ghidra 12.1.2 jars PASS; diff check PASS; independent final review found lifecycle logic sound. Remaining before closure: run focused c64-banking + basic-petscii and full headless suite. Attempts were blocked before execution by the external-execution account usage limit (resets 2026-07-25), not by a test failure.
close_reason: Completed by follow-on session after in-flight agent hit its session limit. Implementation (staged by that agent, reviewed here): AnalyzerRunLog v2 persisted key (one clean verbose retry for Programs polluted by the old failure policy); C64BasicAnalyzer added()->analyze() wrapper so completion is recorded at a single exit (failures/cancellation/exceptions stay retry-eligible, successful work and no-ops complete); BoardBankAnalyzer defers summary + LAST_COMPLETED stamp + completion until the entry/exit structural fingerprint is stable (reachedFixpoint), so phase-2 changing rounds stay verbose and the one summary carries final counts. Validation: orchestrator + independent subagent review clean; focused c64-banking + basic-petscii chunks PASS (new B5 lifecycle criterion demonstrates failure-stays-incomplete + verbose retry); FULL build-and-test.sh check PASS. Known gap noted: C7/C8 cover banking completion + fixpoint predicate but not a BoardBankAnalyzer-specific failure-retry/legacy-key scenario (B5 covers those only for C64BasicAnalyzer).

title: Analyzers: quiet routine logging on re-analysis runs, verbose only on first pass
description: The retromachines analyzers emit routine log output on EVERY added() call -- i.e. every time instructions are (re)disassembled, including manual/incremental disassembly after the initial autoanalysis, not just the first full autoanalyze run. BoardBankAnalyzer is the worst (23 log.appendMsg); C64BasicAnalyzer (8) and others also log per-run summaries. Desired: the first full autoanalyze run may be verbose, but SUBSEQUENT runs should be quiet -- only log messages of Great Importance (genuine warnings/errors), suppressing routine INFO/summary chatter. Approach options: (a) set a marker after the first analysis (a program property / Options flag) and gate routine logging on its absence; (b) detect incremental vs full (added-set size, or whether prior analysis state exists); keep WARNING/error bookmarks always on. Applies to BoardBankAnalyzer + C64BasicAnalyzer + any analyzer with per-run summary logging. Observed by user after the grm-mbm GUI test.

BoardBankAnalyzer now gates six routine progress/summary messages and C64BasicAnalyzer gates its run banner after the initial attempt; all warnings, failures, malformed-input messages, and warning bookmarks remain unconditional. title: SMC: SNES SPC700 upload — cross-processor code extraction to a separate Program
description: Use case 3: SNES games upload SPC700 sound-driver code/data through the APU IO ports ($2140-$2143 handshake protocol) into the sound processor's OWN 64K address space and run it there. Different processor (SPC700 vs 65816), different address space — Ghidra Programs are single-language, so the right deliverable is arguably a SEPARATE Program: recognize/parse the upload (boot-ROM IPL handshake protocol blocks: address+length+data records, well documented on fullsnes/nesdev-adjacent references), extract the transferred image, and materialize a new SPC700-language Program in the project (headless: Program creation API; GUI: an action/script), cross-linked to the source Program (bookmarks/comments at the upload site naming the generated Program and vice versa). STRONG GME TIE-IN: this is exactly the AKAO SNES sound-driver code (FF2/FF3/CT dumpspc.pl lineage in game-music-extraction) — the extracted Program is the disassembly target for the music-driver reverse engineering that motivates the whole toolchain. Design questions: one Program per upload session vs per unique image (games re-upload variants); IPL protocol variants vs game-specific upload loops (AKAO games use their own uploader after boot); where the 'separate Program' convention gets documented for other cross-CPU cases (C64 1541 drive code upload is the same shape!).
notes: 2026-07-12 (user direction) DELIVERABLE SHAPE CORRECTION: output is a SINGLE SPC700 Program (one 64K sound-RAM image) alongside the SNES ROM (65816) Program — NOT one Program per uploaded image. A typical game runs the IPL MULTIPLE times to load separate portions of the SAME SPC700 RAM (e.g. one IPL load transfers the SPC700 driver code, another static instrument/sample data, another filter/echo settings). Recovery model = accumulate ALL IPL transfers into the one SPC700 RAM image at their target addresses (same shape as a fully-populated .spc snapshot). Each ROM-side upload site gets a bookmark cross-linking to the target range it populated. One-language-per-Program still puts SPC700 in its own Program (separate from 65816 ROM), but exactly ONE per game, built from N uploads. Updated docs/smc-survey.md par.5 (grm-1.7.3 Deliverable shape bullet) to match.

comments.author: Chris Bongaarts
comments.text:
PRIMARY CONSUMER OF grm-c9d, confirmed by the user 2026-08-16: "for GME purposes, we will generally
not be working from .spc files, but the game ROM, with reversing providing hints on where the code
is and the entry point ... the cross-platform code upload aspect of 1.7 is all about this."

So this bead, not the .spc loader, is the reason the SPC700 language work is being done. The P3 ->
P2 bump made earlier today stands, and grm-c9d.4 (.spc loader) has been dropped to P4 to match.

EXPLICIT INVITATION RECORDED, worth designing for rather than deferring: "though if analyzers can
find it automatically, all the better." The entry point does not have to arrive as a user-supplied
hint. The IPL handshake transfers address+length+data records and the closing handshake hands over
a start address, so BOTH the target ranges and the entry point are recoverable from the ROM-side
upload code itself. Treat hint-driven entry as the fallback, automatic recovery as the goal --
this is the difference between our result and SPCdra's, which tells the user to run bsnes-plus and
set an S-SMP execute breakpoint by hand.

comments.author: Chris Bongaarts
comments.text:
CORRECTION AND MAJOR FINDING 2026-08-17, from reading the extractor scripts (dumpspc.pl et al,
which sit beside each sample and name the ROM offset). This revises what I recorded earlier.

WHAT I GOT WRONG: I described the .bin container as "the format it is stored in", full stop.
Half right. The [len][addr][data] RECORDS are genuinely the ROM's own upload script, but the
TERMINATOR AND ENTRY POINT ARE SYNTHESIZED BY THE SCRIPTS. E.g. minidumpspc.pl:

    print OUT pack("v", length($buf)), $addr, $buf, pack("v", 0), $addr;

It reuses $addr as the trailing "entry". That fully explains why entry == first block's
destination in every sample -- I had flagged that coincidence as a gap in the corpus, and it
is not a property of the games at all. NO ENTRY POINT IS BEING RECOVERED FROM THE ROM in any
of these; do not build a consumer that trusts that field as an entry point.

THE MULTI-BLOCK EXAMPLE ALREADY EXISTS -- it is F-Zero, and it is why that directory has the
fzspc-*.bin files. fzero/dumpspc.pl is the only one of the four that LOOPS:

    seek IN, 0x008000 + 0x200, 0;
    for (;;) { read 4 bytes -> ($len,$addr); last unless $len > 0; read $len; write piece }

producing five pieces, in upload order:
    0: 0x0500, 624 bytes      3: 0xa080, 10381 bytes
    1: 0x3cc0, 422 bytes      4: 0x07fe, 1 byte
    2: 0x0800, 13306 bytes
Piece 4 being a SINGLE BYTE at 0x07FE is almost certainly a trigger/start write rather than
payload -- exactly the kind of thing an accumulating recovery model must not mistake for code.
fzerospc.bin is NOT the whole upload: minidumpspc.pl re-reads only the 0x0800 chunk from
0x00841e and wraps it. So the corpus already covers the multi-piece case; it was just filed
under a different naming scheme.

THE ROM FORMAT IS NOT UNIFORM ACROSS GAMES, and this is the finding that matters for
grm-1.7.3:

  game   ROM location (script)                          record shape
  ----   --------------------------------------------   -----------------------------------
  fzero  fzero.smc    0x008000 + 0x200 hdr               LOOP of [u16 len][u16 addr][data],
                                                         terminated by len==0. Real block list.
  lem    lemmings.smc 8*0x8000 + (0xe7d7-0x8000)         [u16 len][u16 addr][data], single
                      = 0x467D7, and NOTE no +0x200      record (script does not loop)
  som    som1.smc     0x030748 + 0x200 hdr               [u16 len][data] -- NO ADDRESS FIELD.
                                                         Script hardcodes dest 0x0200.
  ff3    f_fan3.fig   0x05070e + 0x200 hdr               [u16 len][data] -- NO ADDRESS FIELD.
                                                         Script hardcodes dest 0x0200.

So on the two AKAO titles the DESTINATION IS NOT IN THE DATA AT ALL -- it lives in the 65816
uploader code, and the human extracting it supplied 0x0200 by hand. A static parser cannot
recover it from the block stream because it is not there.

THIS IS DIRECT EVIDENCE FOR docs/smc-survey.md's HYBRID RULING, and sharpens it. The survey
proposed a static tier ("the $2140-43 handshake carries documented address+length+data
records") plus a generic emulation tier. These four samples show the split is not a
convenience but a necessity: F-Zero's static block list is parseable with no emulation at all,
while SoM and FF3 need the uploader's CODE to know where the bytes go. Any plan that assumes
one universal ROM layout will work on F-Zero and silently produce address-less blobs on the
Square titles.

Also worth noting the SMC header inconsistency (three files need +0x200, lemmings.smc does
not) -- a real extractor must detect the 512-byte copier header rather than assume it.

AKAO UPLOADS ARE CODE ONLY. Per the owner: AKAO drivers stream instrument samples on demand
as songs play, so these extracts contain no BRR sample data. That explains the size gap --
som 5016 / ff3 6071 bytes versus F-Zero's 13306+10381 across two large pieces, where the
non-AKAO driver ships its samples up front. Consequence for us: an AKAO extract is almost
pure code, which makes it the BETTER disassembly target, while an F-Zero-style image needs
code/data separation before it is useful.

SECOND ASSET FOUND, and it may be worth as much as the binaries: nine ANNOTATED REFERENCE
DISASSEMBLIES exist in the corpus -- ct, ff3, ff5, fzero, gradius3, lem, mario, sd3, som
(*spc.dis, 32K-204K each). They carry addresses, bytes, mnemonics AND hand comments:

    0200 20         CLRP               ; dpage = 0
    0201 C0         DI                 ; interrupts off
    0202 CD FF      MOV     X,#$FF
    0204 BD         MOV     SP,X       ; SP = $(01)FF
    ...
    020B D0 FB      BNE     $0208      ; zero $00-$EF

My independent hand-decode of somspc.bin matched somspc.dis line for line. These are usable
two ways: as GROUND TRUTH for grm-c9d.3's disassembly (diff our listing against a known-good
one over thousands of real instructions, far beyond what Spc700LanguageTest's 8 encodings
pin), and as a symbol/comment source for AKAO analysis. Worth its own bead if we act on it.

CORPUS STATUS: four parsed samples (som, ff3, fzero, lem), all consuming their bytes exactly;
multi-piece case COVERED by fzero's five pieces; entry-point recovery still uncovered and now
known to be uncoverable from these files by construction.

comments.author: Chris Bongaarts
comments.text:
THE UPLOADER IS ALREADY DISASSEMBLED AND HAND-ANNOTATED, in the owner's own pre-Ghidra work.
Found 2026-08-17 in Z:/git/game-music-extraction/snes/*/ alongside the .bin extracts.

WORKFLOW CONTEXT FROM THE OWNER, which is what makes this corpus interesting rather than just
old: his pre-Ghidra method was to run CHUNKS of the ROM through a disassembler, hand-analyze
the listing to find the music-relevant code, then extract and disassemble the SPC side. That
is precisely the pipeline this bead automates. So the 65816 .dis files are a RECORD OF A
MANUAL RUN OF THIS BEAD'S JOB, and the hand comments mark the path he actually took through
each ROM.

CONCRETE FIND -- Secret of Mana's IPL uploader, som/som03.dis at $03/004A:

    03004a f0 32        BEQ $007e        ; wait for SPC to initialize
    03005f 8d 41 21     STA $2141        ; APU I/O Port
    030064 8d 40 21     STA $2140        ; APU I/O Port
    03007e ec 40 21     CPX $2140        ; APU I/O Port
    030086 af 14 00 c3  LDA $c30014
    03008a 8d 42 21     STA $2142        ; APU I/O Port
    03008d af 15 00 c3  LDA $c30015
    030091 8d 43 21     STA $2143        ; send dest of 1st block to APU2/3
    030094 a9 cc        LDA #$cc
    030096 8d 41 21     STA $2141        ; APU I/O Port
    030099 8d 40 21     STA $2140        ; APU I/O Port
    03009c cd 40 21     CMP $2140        ; APU I/O Port
    0300a4 bf 08 00 c3  LDA $c30008,X

REFINES WHAT I RECORDED EARLIER, and I had it slightly wrong. I said the destination on the
Square titles "is not in the data at all -- it lives in the 65816 uploader code". More
precisely: THE DESTINATION IS IN ROM, at $C3/0014-0015, but ONLY THE CODE SAYS WHERE. It sits
in a small header separate from the payload, which the uploader streams from $C3/0008,X. A
static parser cannot find it by walking the block stream, because it is not inline -- it has
to follow the uploader's absolute-long loads. The owner's own hand comment "send dest of 1st
block to APU2/3" confirms the reading independently.

This STRENGTHENS the hybrid ruling in docs/smc-survey.md rather than changing it: F-Zero's
ROM genuinely carries a self-describing [len][addr][data] block list that static parsing can
walk unaided, while SoM needs the uploader's code read to locate a header at a game-specific
address. Same conclusion, sharper evidence: the variation is not "some games are harder", it
is that the address of the address is only knowable from code.

APU PORT COVERAGE ACROSS THE CORPUS, i.e. where the uploaders are, all pre-located:
    som03.dis 107 lines   som02 35   som00 3   som01 1
    ff3: f3-05 85, f3-02 28, f3-01 14, f3-00/03/06/07 ~5 each
    fzero00.dis 17        lem08.dis 87, lem00.dis 4
Concentration is the signal -- the bank with ~100 $2140-43 references is the uploader/driver
bank in every one of these titles.

TWO USES FOR THIS BEAD:
 1. Test expectations. "Did our extractor find the uploader at $03/004A in Secret of Mana,
    and recover dest=$0200 from $C3/0014?" is now a checkable question with a known answer,
    for four titles.
 2. Heuristic design. The hand comments show WHAT A HUMAN KEYED ON when locating this code --
    the $2140-43 write cluster, the handshake wait loop, the #$CC magic. Those are exactly the
    recognizer inputs an analyzer needs, and they come with a worked example per title.

CAVEAT ON COVERAGE, important: these listings are NOT complete verified disassemblies. The
owner disassembled the chunks he needed and annotated only what was music-relevant. ABSENCE
of a comment means "not examined", NOT "not interesting" -- so the files are evidence of
presence, never of absence, and no coverage metric should be derived from them.

comments.author: Chris Bongaarts
comments.text:
CORRECTION on AKAO sample handling, and it carries a design consequence for the recovery model.

I have now had two goes at this and both were too coarse. Precisely, per the owner:

  AKAO uploads samples AS NEEDED FOR BACKGROUND MUSIC. There are ALSO sound-effect samples and
  the like which are PERMANENTLY RESIDENT.

So it is not "AKAO extracts are code only" (my first version), nor "early AKAO uploads samples
up front while later AKAO streams" (my second, from FF2's eight blocks). EVERY AKAO version
does BOTH: a resident set goes up in the initial upload, and BGM sample data is streamed per
song thereafter. What differs between titles is HOW MUCH is resident, not whether streaming
happens.

That is consistent with everything measured: FF2's initial upload carries three sample blocks
plus three BRR directory tables (~9.5 KB of sample data) because its resident set is large,
while SoM's 5016 bytes and FF3's 6071 are essentially pure code with a smaller or separately
loaded resident set. Same architecture, different split.

THE CONSEQUENCE FOR grm-1.7.3's RECOVERY MODEL, which is the reason this is worth writing down
rather than being trivia: docs/smc-survey.md:171 rules that recovery should ACCUMULATE ALL IPL
TRANSFERS INTO ONE 64K SPC700 RAM IMAGE, on the model of an .spc snapshot. That is right for
CODE and for the resident set, but it is NOT a complete description of the machine's life --
BGM sample regions are OVERWRITTEN REPEATEDLY AT RUNTIME, once per song change. An accumulated
image is therefore a POINT IN TIME, and some address ranges are legitimately multi-valued over
the program's execution.

Practical implications, none of which invalidate the accumulate model but all of which qualify it:
 * A region that later gets streamed over is not "the" contents of that address -- labelling it
   as settled data would be wrong. It is one occupant of a slot, which is precisely the banked-
   occupant situation this project already models with overlays elsewhere.
 * Code and the resident set are stable and safe to treat as the program; streamed BGM sample
   regions are transient buffers and are better modelled as such (an uninitialized or
   overlay-style region) than as recovered bytes.
 * FF2's notes.txt gives the taxonomy to key on -- each block is tagged code / samples / BRR
   directory table, and the directory tables say which sample region they serve. A recovery
   pass that preserved those roles would be able to make exactly this distinction, rather than
   producing 64K of undifferentiated bytes.
 * The BRR directory tables are the structural hook: a dir table pointing into a region is
   evidence that region is sample data rather than code, available statically.

Do not read this as an argument to change the accumulate model. It is an argument to record
PROVENANCE AND ROLE per region while accumulating, so a later consumer can tell "this is the
driver" from "this is whatever song happened to be loaded when the snapshot was taken".

comments.author: Chris Bongaarts
comments.text:
SCOPING NOTE on the preceding comment: THE ON-DEMAND SAMPLE LOADING IS SPECIFIC TO THE AKAO
FAMILY. Per the owner, other drivers may have approached sample loading entirely differently,
and he does not recall how most of them handled it.

So the corrected model above -- resident set up front, BGM samples streamed per song -- is a
statement about AKAO (Square: FF2, FF3, FF5, SoM, SD3, Chrono Trigger), NOT about SNES audio
drivers generally. Do not carry it over to F-Zero, Lemmings, Gradius III, Super Mario World or
anything else in the corpus.

WHAT THAT MEANS FOR THE RECOVERY MODEL: the design has to tolerate BOTH ends of a spectrum
without knowing in advance which a title sits at.

  * A FULLY-RESIDENT driver uploads everything once and never streams. For those, the
    accumulate-into-one-64K-image model is COMPLETE, not a point in time, and every recovered
    region is stable. F-Zero looks like a plausible candidate -- its five blocks total ~24 KB
    including two large ones, which is a lot to be pure code -- but that is an inference from
    size, NOT a measurement, and it should be checked rather than assumed.
  * An AKAO-style driver streams, so parts of the image are transient. Accumulation is a
    snapshot.

The practical upshot is that "is this region stable code/data or a transient buffer?" is a
PER-DRIVER question with no universal answer, and nothing in the ROM header or the upload
format announces it. Two honest options for a recovery pass: recover the accumulated image and
label regions by evidence (a BRR directory table pointing into a region is static evidence it
is sample data, per the previous comment), or emulate far enough to observe whether a region
is rewritten. Do not build in an assumption either way.

AND DO NOT SPEND AGENT TOKENS RECONSTRUCTING THIS FROM THE ROMS. Determining how Lemmings or
Gradius III handled sample loading is hand reverse-engineering of a specific driver -- the
class of work CLAUDE.md designates as cheaper for a human with a disassembler than for an
agent running build/measure cycles. If it becomes load-bearing for a design decision, ASK,
and note that the owner's own recollection has already been offered and does not cover it.

comments.author: Chris Bongaarts
comments.text:
WHERE AKAO's SAMPLE MEMORY MANAGEMENT ACTUALLY LIVES: THE 65816 SIDE, NOT THE SPC700.

Per the owner (2026-08-17), for the AKAO family at least: the song format carries information
about which samples a song needs. The 65816 uploads those samples AND writes the BRR directory
entries that map them to the instrument slots the song format references. The SPC700 driver
then simply knows that to play instrument N it plays sample M -- the indirection is already
resolved for it.

THIS CHANGES WHERE THE INTERESTING CODE IS, and it is close to the opposite of what an
SPC700-first approach would assume:

 * An SPC700-only analysis WILL NOT FIND SAMPLE MANAGEMENT. There is nothing to find there --
   the driver reads a directory someone else populated and writes DSP registers. All the
   allocation, residency and mapping logic is ROM-side.
 * THE BRR DIRECTORY IN SPC RAM HAS NO WRITER VISIBLE IN THE SPC IMAGE. A static analysis of
   an uploaded image will see a table that nothing in that image ever writes. That is not a
   gap in the analysis -- its provenance is genuinely cross-processor. An analyzer should say
   so rather than leaving it as an unexplained data region.
 * grm-1.7.3's cross-processor extraction therefore matters twice over: the ROM side holds
   both the song->sample manifest and the code that builds the mapping. Recovering only the
   SPC700 image recovers the player, not the thing that decides what it plays.

CORRECTION TO MY EARLIER CLAIM, which was too strong. I wrote that "a BRR directory table
pointing into a region is static evidence that region is sample data rather than code,
available statically". That holds ONLY for directories present in the uploaded image -- i.e.
the RESIDENT set, like FF2's blocks 02/05/07 which are uploaded as dir tables alongside their
sample blocks. For STREAMED BGM samples the directory entries are written at runtime by the
65816 and are NOT in the upload at all, so the static hook simply does not exist for them. The
two facts fit together: resident samples ship with their directories, streamed ones get theirs
written later.

USEFUL STRUCTURE, for whenever this gets built:
 * A BRR directory entry is 4 bytes -- two 16-bit pointers, sample start and loop point.
 * The directory's base address is held in the DSP's DIR register, so the table's location is
   discoverable from a DSP register write rather than having to be guessed.
 * Instrument slot -> sample index is the mapping the 65816 writes; the song data references
   instrument slots, so reading song data without that mapping gives you slot numbers with no
   meaning attached.

SCOPE, AGAIN: this is an AKAO-family statement. Other drivers may divide the work between the
two processors completely differently, and the owner does not recall how most of them did it
(see the preceding scoping comment). Do not assume ROM-side sample management for anything
outside AKAO without checking, and treat "which side manages samples" as a per-driver question.

comments.author: Chris Bongaarts
comments.text:
CORRECTION to the preceding comment, which over-claimed. I wrote that "the 65816 uploads those
samples AND writes the BRR directory entries", and then built an analyzer expectation on top
of it ("the BRR directory has no writer visible in the SPC image"). That second step is NOT
established. Per the owner, it has been too long to recall whether the SPC-side driver
calculates the directory itself or the 65816 sends it as a chunk of data. Either is possible.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY KNOWN, separated by confidence:

CERTAIN:
 * The SPC700's role in sample management is to RECEIVE the samples from the 65816. The
   allocation decision -- which samples a song needs -- is made ROM-side.
 * THE 65816 RUNS THE SHOW AND THE SPC700 ACTS IN A "SLAVE" MODE. This is the durable
   architectural point, and unlike the sample-residency detail IT IS TYPICAL OF MOST SNES
   GAMES, not an AKAO peculiarity. It is the one generalization in this whole thread that the
   owner has stated broadly rather than scoped to a driver family.

LIKELY:
 * AKAO uses its own custom signalling protocol for these runtime transfers, but the upload
   MECHANISM is thought to be nearly the same as the boot-time IPL process. If so, a runtime
   sample upload looks structurally like an IPL upload, which is directly useful to
   grm-1.7.3: the same recognizer may serve both, and the accumulate-all-transfers model
   would naturally pick up runtime sample loads as well as the boot image.

UNKNOWN, and to be treated as an open question rather than filled in by inference:
 * Whether the BRR directory is computed by the SPC700 driver or sent by the 65816 as data.
   MY PREVIOUS COMMENT ASSERTED THE LATTER; that assertion should be disregarded.
 * Consequently the analyzer expectation I derived from it -- "a directory table with no
   writer in the SPC image is normal and cross-processor" -- is ALSO not established. It may
   be true, or the driver may build the table itself and the writer will be right there.
   Do not encode either as an assumption; if it matters, it is answerable by looking at one
   driver's code, which is a small, well-defined hand task rather than a design premise.

WHY THE MASTER/SLAVE POINT IS THE ONE TO BUILD ON: it says the SPC700 image is, on its own, an
incomplete artifact for almost any SNES title -- it is the subordinate half of a two-processor
system whose decisions are made elsewhere. That is an argument for grm-1.7.3's cross-processor
framing generally, independent of AKAO, and it does not depend on any of the uncertain details
above. It also sets expectations for what SPC700 decompilation can deliver: a faithful player,
with the "why" living in the ROM.

comments.author: Chris Bongaarts
comments.text:
THIRD ASSET IN THE CORPUS: THE CROSS-PROCESSOR COMMAND PROTOCOL, DOCUMENTED ON BOTH SIDES.

Per the owner (2026-08-17), at least a couple of the disassemblies carry comments where he
worked out the communication between the two processors -- "I'm sending song data", "play this
song", "set this variable used by the sequence interpreter", "enable the drum track because
Mario is on Yoshi". Notes exist on BOTH the SPC and 65816 sides in those cases, and at minimum
THE CODE AREAS ARE MECHANICALLY LOCATABLE: the IO register accesses on each side.

THE TWO SIDES OF ONE PORT PAIR:
  65816 side: $2140-$2143
  SPC700 side: $00F4-$00F7 (direct page)
Same four physical registers seen from opposite ends. The owner's own comment on ff3spc.dis
line 09E1 makes the link explicit -- "MOV X,$F4  ; check 2140" -- which is exactly the
cross-reference an analyzer would need to relate the two Programs.

MEASURED, SPC SIDE (direct-page $F4-$F7 only; an earlier count of mine was inflated by
matching absolute addresses like $F600+X, which are ordinary memory, not ports):

    sd3   113 refs,  4 commented        g3      5 refs, 0 commented
    ct     87 refs,  0 commented        fzero   2 refs, 0 commented
    ff3    78 refs, 15 commented        lem     0 refs, 0 commented
    som    60 refs, 13 commented        mario   0 refs, 0 commented
    ff5    49 refs,  5 commented

65816 side, from the earlier scan of $2140-43 references: som03 107, lem08 87, f3-05 85,
fzero00 17. The bank with ~100 references is the driver/uploader bank in every title.

RICHEST PROTOCOL DOCUMENTATION IS ff3 AND som, on both sides -- ff3 15 commented SPC-side port
lines and 85 on the 65816 side (f3-05); som 13 and 107 (som03). Those two are where the
protocol was actually worked out. Samples of the SPC-side comments:

    02A4 DA F6   MOVW $F6,YA     ; write $DD and $52 or $AD to APU2/3
    02AA DA F4   MOVW $F4,YA     ; write #$00 and $7B to APU0/1
    09E1 F8 F4   MOV  X,$F4      ; check 2140
    (section header)             ; process CPU cmd $F4

AN OPEN QUESTION, NOT A CONCLUSION: lem and mario show ZERO direct-page port references in
their SPC listings, and fzero/g3 show 2 and 5. A working driver must communicate somehow, so
the plausible explanations are (a) those listings cover only part of the image, (b) those
drivers use a different notation the grep missed, or (c) they genuinely poll differently.
Do not infer "these drivers don't use the ports". Given the repeated lesson in this corpus
that measurable artifacts under-determine the explanation, this is a question for the owner or
for reading one of those listings, not something to settle by more grepping.

WHY THIS MATTERS BEYOND ARCHAEOLOGY: the protocol IS the interface between the two Programs
that grm-1.7.3 will produce. Recovering an SPC700 image gives a player whose inputs are
opaque command bytes; the protocol comments say what those bytes MEAN. Concretely useful for:
 * naming the command dispatch table on the SPC side (ff3 has an explicit "process CPU cmd $F4"
   section, and the FF2 notes.txt records a full dispatch map of command -> handler address)
 * annotating the 65816 side's writes with their intent
 * giving a future analyzer a target: a $2140-43 write cluster on one side and a $F4-$F7 read
   dispatch on the other are two halves of one protocol, and relating them across Programs is
   exactly the cross-processor reference problem this project already thinks about for banking.

Consistent with the master/slave architecture recorded on grm-1.7.3: the 65816 issues commands
and the SPC obeys, so the command vocabulary is the SPC driver's real API.

title: Self-modifying code strategies: run-from-elsewhere, decrypt-on-the-fly, cross-processor code upload
description: Umbrella for making the extension useful on the self-modifying-code patterns retro software actually uses — an axis Ghidra has traditionally handled poorly (static listing assumes bytes at an address are THE code). Three concrete use-case families (children), plus a cross-cutting question: the Ghidra Debugger's emulator/trace machinery may be leverageable for all of them (execute the copier/decryptor in the p-code emulator, capture the resulting memory image, feed it back into static analysis) — traditionally SMC was hopeless statically, but Debugger-assisted 'run it, then analyze what it produced' changes the economics. Design tension to resolve early: which patterns deserve STATIC modeling (descriptor-driven, like banking) vs EMULATION-ASSISTED recovery vs manual workflow documentation. Relationship to banking engine (grm-5tl): banking changes which pre-existing bytes are visible; SMC creates NEW bytes at analysis time — different problem, but the overlay/alternate-view plumbing and the analyzer-pass architecture are shared infrastructure.
notes: 2026-07-12 grm-1.7.4 survey COMPLETE — design tension RESOLVED, full findings in docs/smc-survey.md. Machinery: EmulatorHelper is @Deprecated(since 12.1, forRemoval=true); all emulation work targets ghidra.pcode.emu.PcodeEmulator + PcodeEmulationCallbacks (readUninitialized = IO fault policy hook, dataWritten = exact dirty-set capture) + EmulatorUtilities.loadProgram (plain-emulator harness, no Trace needed). Interpreted emulator is SMC-safe by construction (SleighInstructionDecoder re-decodes each instruction from live state; avoid JIT emulator for SMC). In-tree precedent: EmuX86DeobfuscateExampleScript. DEBUGGER (per user direction, evaluated first-class): pure-emulation mode + GUI Copy Into Program = the manual/interactive tier (document in grm-fy0); headless Trace round-trip buys nothing over direct Memory.setBytes; TraceRmi retro connector (VICE/Mesen) does not exist and stays NO-GO until demonstrated need — VICE .vsf snapshot import is the cheap 80% (real-hardware-fidelity memory image, zero protocol work). Approach split: 1.7.1 STATIC now; 1.7.2 emulation pilot; 1.7.3 static-first with SPC700 language sourcing as new prerequisite (stock Ghidra has NO SPC700 sleigh — SPCdra is the community candidate). Shared EmulationRecovery harness bead created; reuses the same PcodeEmulationCallbacks layer the banking vision picked for L4 (§7.1) — one callback stack serves both features.

title: Release-build strategy on GitHub (Actions matrix across supported Ghidra versions)
description: Set up automated release builds for ghidra-retro-machines on GitHub. Reference sketch = kylewlacy/GhidraNes (.github/workflows/): a reusable _build.yml (on: workflow_call) building with a matrix of ~19 Ghidra versions (10.3 through 12.1) via the antoniovazquezblanco/setup-ghidra@v2.1.0 action (installs Ghidra + exports GHIDRA_INSTALL_DIR env var), temurin Java 21, gradle -PGHIDRA_INSTALL_DIR=..., then renames dist/*.zip to ghidra_<ver>_<sha>_<date>_<name>.zip and uploads as artifacts; release.yml triggers on tag push v*, calls _build, downloads merged artifacts, and creates a DRAFT release with gh release create --generate-notes + gh release upload; ci.yml reuses the same _build on ordinary pushes. Adaptations needed for GRM: (1) our build.gradle checks the GHIDRA_INSTALL_DIR env var FIRST, which is exactly what setup-ghidra sets — so CI works naturally, no -P needed; (2) matrix should start narrow (12.1.x we actually support) and grow deliberately — sleigh compile + GDT JavaExec tasks may not be version-portable as far back as GhidraNes goes; (3) consider running tools/banktest/run-banktest.sh (analyzeHeadless, works on ubuntu) as a CI quality gate before release assets are published. TRIGGER MECHANISM IS OPEN: user finds tag pushing clunky as a downstream fork — evaluate alternatives: workflow_dispatch with a version input (workflow tags + drafts the release itself, one button in the UI), 'release: published' trigger (draft the release in the UI first, action builds+attaches assets), or push-to-release-branch. Pick whichever makes cutting a release a single low-ceremony step.
design: TRIGGER DECIDED (user, 2026-07-12): workflow_dispatch to start. release.yml takes a version input (e.g. '0.3.0'), runs the _build matrix, then tags and creates the DRAFT release itself (gh release create --generate-notes + upload assets) -- one button in the Actions UI, no local tag push. Tag creation happens IN the workflow from the dispatched ref, so the fork's local clone never needs to push tags. Keep the trigger swappable: structure release.yml so switching to 'release: published' later is just changing the on: block + reading the version from the release tag instead of the input. ci.yml on ordinary pushes reuses the same workflow_call _build.
notes:
Requested by user 2026-07-11. GhidraNes workflow files fetched and verified 2026-07-11 (repo kylewlacy/GhidraNes, default branch main). setup-ghidra action needs auth_token: secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN to avoid API rate limits when downloading Ghidra releases.

VERSION-SUPPORT POLICY (user, 2026-07-11): Ghidra will install/keep using an extension built against a different version — it does NOT proactively check compatibility, so a mismatched build may work or break depending on API drift. For the extensions we care about (mostly loaders), the biggest breakage so far is the 11->12 breaking change to the Loader load() method signature. HARD FLOOR = Ghidra 12.0: we will NOT support the <=11 load() API — working around it is a pain (see how GhidraNes contorts to span both). So the matrix may be a small subset, possibly even one build serving several versions. PROCEDURE: check back-support starting at 12.0 and work FORWARD, running the banktest suite against each release to find the true minimum version that works (compat = suite passes, not just compiles). If we find critical dependencies on behavior introduced post-12.0 (candidates to check: ImporterSettings record shape, CommentType enum, SleighCompile invocation, MemoryBlockUtils signatures), DISCUSS each with the user before deciding to work around it vs. raising the floor — do not silently add compat shims.
