comments.text:
CORRECTION to the previous comment's date reading. Per the owner, a single file's mtime is
unreliable (his touch of ff3 may have been accidental); the OLDEST file in a title's directory
is the better indicator of when work on it started. Re-measured directory-wide:

  dir        files  oldest       newest
  ff3        17     2001-02-22   2026-07-18
  lem        14     2001-03-11   2001-03-18
  som        16     2001-03-22   2001-04-07
  sd3        15     2001-03-22   2001-04-17
  ct         10     2001-03-22   2026-05-17
  ff5        14     2001-03-22   2025-12-20
  gradius3   12     2001-03-22   2026-02-21
  mario      10     2001-03-22   2017-06-27
  fzero      14     2001-03-22   2001-08-26

TWO FINDINGS, THE FIRST OF WHICH REVERSES WHAT I WROTE BEFORE.

1. ff3 IS THE EARLIEST TITLE, NOT THE MOST RECENT. 2001-02-22, a clear month before anything
   else. Its 2026-07-18 mtime was the incidental touch the owner warned about, and I had read
   it as "recently revisited, therefore most developed". Wrong direction.

   This STRENGTHENS the owner's account rather than complicating it: ff3 has the MOST hand
   comments in the corpus (476 singletons, 16.9% density), which is exactly what you expect
   from the first title tackled -- everything had to be discovered and was worth writing down.
   The prior comment's conclusion (start with ff3) survives, but for the opposite reason.

2. THE 2001-03-22 CLUSTER IS AN ARTIFACT, NOT SEVEN SIMULTANEOUS STARTS. Seven directories
   sharing one oldest-date almost certainly means a bulk copy or disk migration stamped them
   all, so for those titles the start date is simply LOST and the oldest-file heuristic does
   not apply. Do not read that date as when work began on som/sd3/ct/ff5/gradius3/mario/fzero.

   Their .dis mtimes all postdate the cluster and so probably do reflect real work order:
   som 03-26, sd3 04-01, ct 04-13, ff5 04-13, gradius3 05-21, mario 08-23, fzero 08-26.
   Treat that as a plausible sequence, not a measured one.

NET EFFECT ON THE DENSITY HYPOTHESIS: it holds up. Earliest title (ff3) is the most annotated;
the two latest large ones (gradius3 05-21 at 6.4%, fzero 08-26 at 3.8%) are the sparsest. The
mid-cluster titles sit between at 12-16%. Still a tendency rather than a law -- mario is late
and dense (17.9%) though small -- and still supporting NO negative inference, per the previous
comment.

PRIORITY ORDER FOR THIS BEAD IS UNCHANGED, since it was set by hand-comment count rather than
by date: ff3 (476), ff5 (353), som (335), ct (326). It is merely now better justified.

GENERAL LESSON worth carrying beyond this bead: filesystem mtimes in a decades-old corpus are
evidence about the FILES, not about the work. Cross-check any date-derived inference against a
second signal -- here, comment counts and the directory-wide range -- before relying on it.

comments.author: Chris Bongaarts
comments.text:
BETTER DATE SOURCE: INTERNAL HEADER COMMENTS IN THE .pl SCRIPTS. Per the owner, the uniform
2001-03-22 filesystem cluster is a mass copy to a server, and the Perl scripts carry their own
dates. Confirmed and much more informative -- but with one confound that must be applied.

CHRONOLOGY FROM INTERNAL DATES:

  ff3        25 Feb 2001   ff3mus.pl        (dir oldest file is 22 Feb, consistent)
  lem        March 2001    lemmus.pl
  som        25-27 Mar     sominflate.pl 25 Mar, sommus.pl / sommustxt.pl 27 Mar
  sd3        1-6 Apr       songidx.pl 1 Apr, sd3txt.pl 6 Apr
  gradius3   16 May 2001   g3mus.pl
  mario      19 Aug 2001   mariomus.pl
  fzero      25 Aug 2001   fzmus.pl
  ct         (see below)   ctmus.pl / cttxt.pl both say 25 Feb 2001
  ff5, ff2, lufia          no date headers found

THE CONFOUND -- INHERITED HEADERS. "25 Feb 2001" appears in THREE titles: ff3mus.pl, ctmus.pl
and sd3mus.pl. These are all Square/AKAO games with near-identical driver structure, and sd3's
OTHER scripts are dated 1 and 6 April. So the header date travelled with the file when a
script was copied as the starting point for the next title, and was not re-dated. ff3 is the
genuine 25 Feb original; ct's and sd3's mus.pl dates are derived and say nothing about when
those titles were worked.

RULE: prefer a title's EARLIEST NON-mus.pl script, or corroborate a mus.pl date against a
sibling script, before treating it as a start date. A date shared across titles is a copy, the
same way the shared filesystem date was.

NET: ff3 IS FIRST, on three independent signals now -- earliest directory mtime (22 Feb),
earliest internal date (25 Feb), and the only unambiguous holder of that date. And it has the
MOST hand comments in the corpus (476, 16.9%). The owner's account (early work recorded more,
later work recorded less because he knew what to look for) fits the corrected ordering better
than it fit the filesystem one:

  ff3       Feb   476 hand comments  16.9%   <- first, densest
  som       Mar   335                15.9%
  sd3       Apr   279                13.3%
  gradius3  May   269                 6.4%
  mario     Aug   275                17.9%   <- outlier, but a small file (1780 lines)
  fzero     Aug   179                 3.8%   <- last, sparsest

Still a tendency rather than a law, and still supporting NO negative inference about
uncommented regions. Part of gradius3's and fzero's low density is that they are non-AKAO
drivers carrying uploaded sample DATA that was never going to be commented.

CORPUS IS LARGER THAN PREVIOUSLY RECORDED: eleven title directories, not nine -- ct, ff2, ff3,
ff5, fzero, gradius3, lem, lufia, mario, sd3, som. ff2 and lufia were missed earlier because
they have no *spc.dis; they may still hold ROM-side listings or scripts worth reading.

PRIORITY FOR THIS BEAD UNCHANGED (it was set on hand-comment counts, not dates): ff3, ff5,
som, ct.

comments.author: Chris Bongaarts
comments.text:
THE STRONGEST COUNTEREXAMPLE TO RANKING BY COMMENT DENSITY, and it lands on the origin title.

Per the owner (2026-08-17): he worked FF2 FIRST and FF3 second, the rest after -- and MOST OF
THE FF2 SPC ANALYSIS WAS DONE BY HAND ON A PAPER PRINTOUT, in pencil.

So the most thoroughly analyzed title in the corpus is among the least annotated on disk:
ff2spc.txt carries 132 commented lines out of 2224. Ranking targets by comment density would
place the ORIGIN title near the bottom, which is precisely backwards -- and no inspection of
the files could have revealed it. Only the owner's memory did.

Two consequences for this bead:

 1. The priority order (ff3, ff5, som, ct -- by hand-comment count) stands as a way to find
    ANNOTATED comparison material, but must not be read as a ranking of which listings are
    trustworthy or well-understood. Those are different properties and this is the proof.

 2. READ THE NOTES FILES, NOT JUST THE LISTINGS. ff2/notes.txt (30 KB) holds the structured
    findings that never made it into ff2spc.txt -- including the complete 8-block upload map
    with each block's role (code / samples / BRR directory table) and the execution address.
    That is the single most informative artifact found in the corpus so far, and it is in a
    file this bead's original method would never have opened. Check for notes.txt / work.txt /
    a docs subdirectory in EVERY title directory before concluding anything from a listing's
    sparseness.

This also revises the date chronology one more time: the corpus starts MAY 2000 with ff2, not
Feb 2001 with ff3. ff3 is second, not first. The density trend across the remaining titles is
unaffected, but ff2 sits outside it entirely -- maximum effort, minimum digital annotation.

comments.author: Chris Bongaarts
comments.text:
HARNESS BUILT AND FIRST FULL RUN DONE. HEADLINE: 29,236 INSTRUCTIONS COMPARED ACROSS ALL NINE
LISTINGS, 254 OF 256 OPCODES EXERCISED, 16 RESIDUAL DISAGREEMENTS -- AND NONE OF THEM ARE OURS.
Five of the nine listings (ff5, som, ct, sd3, fzero) agree with SPC700:LE:16:retro on every
single instruction.

WHAT WAS BUILT
  src/test/java/retromachines/corpus/DisListing.java        -- listing parser
  src/test/java/retromachines/corpus/Spc700DisCorpusTest.java -- differential + reports
  build.gradle task spc700DisCorpusTest, chunk `spc700-dis-corpus` in build-and-test.sh
  env var GRM_SPC700_DIS_CORPUS (the snes/ dir); Assume-skips when unset

  GRM_SPC700_DIS_CORPUS=Z:/git/game-music-extraction/snes \
    bash tools/banktest/build-and-test.sh check spc700-dis-corpus

It is a REPORTING tier, deliberately not a gate, and the class doc says so at length: it writes
per-row TSVs to build/spc700-dis-corpus/ and asserts only that every byte sequence the listings
call code disassembles at all. It Assume-SKIPS when the env var is unset rather than refusing
loudly like the vector tier -- there is no green here worth protecting. The framing from this
bead (leads, not truth; never "fix" the language to match a .dis) is written into the class doc,
the chunk comment in build-and-test.sh, docs/testing.md and CLAUDE.md, so it survives the
session.

METHOD DECISION WORTH RECORDING: THE LISTING'S OWN CODE/DATA SPLIT DRIVES THE DISASSEMBLY.
The seed set is exactly the addresses a listing marks as instructions, with followFlow OFF, and
the restricted set is every address it covers at all. So each instruction start is decoded on
its own terms and Ghidra never wanders into a pointer table. That keeps row-to-row alignment
exact and makes this a test of the DECODE TABLE rather than of flow recovery -- which is what
the bead wanted, since the vectors already cover semantics and nothing covered decode text
beyond Spc700LanguageTest's 8 hand-picked encodings.

FULL RESULTS (code rows / undecoded / split / lenDiff / textDiff)
  ff3       2657   0  3  3  10
  ff5       2695   0  0  0   0
  som       2276   0  0  0   0
  ct        3152   0  0  0   0
  sd3       2435   0  0  0   0
  gradius3  6745   0 12  1   5
  mario     1643   0  0  0   0
  lem       1262   0  0  1   1
  fzero     6355   0  0  0   0

OPCODE COVERAGE: 254/256. Only 59 (EOR (X),(Y)) and 6A (AND1 C,/dp.bit) never appear as an
instruction head anywhere in the corpus. Twelve more appear only once or twice (19 41 47 4A 53
54 55 56 57 61 71 DF). Note WHERE the breadth comes from: gradius3 (244 distinct opcodes) and
fzero (240) are the non-AKAO drivers that upload sample data with their code, so a large part of
their "code" is BRR data being disassembled as junk by both tools. That junk is not worthless
for this purpose -- it is near-uniform bytes exercising the decode table far more evenly than
real code does, and both tools agreeing on it is real evidence. The five AKAO listings sit at
137-148 distinct opcodes each.

THE 16 RESIDUAL ROWS, FULLY TRIAGED. TWO CATEGORIES, NEITHER A DEFECT ON OUR SIDE.

(A) EIGHT ROWS ARE DELIBERATE OVERLAPPING INSTRUCTION STREAMS -- and this is the most
    interesting thing the exercise turned up, because the owner ANNOTATED THEM BY HAND at the
    time. ff3spc.dis:

      029F E5         MOV  A,$ADEB   ; pseudo op to skip instruction
      02A0 EB AD      MOV  Y,$AD
      0345 E8         MOV  A,#$FC    ; pseudo-op skip
      0346 FC         INC  Y
      0C75 8D         MOV  Y,#$60    ; "skip" next instruction
      0C76 60         CLRC

    The classic trick: a 2- or 3-byte opcode whose immediate operand IS the next instruction,
    so falling through executes the skip-op and branching to +1 executes the real one. BOTH
    decodes are correct, of different entry points, and the listing shows both -- which is why
    they cannot both be rows in a flat comparison. Note the listing's byte column shows only ONE
    byte on the skip-op line, so the file is internally inconsistent there by construction; that
    is the annotation working as intended, not an error.

    The other five (gradius3 2BF9, 2C5E, 2DAF, 2DB0, 2DB1) are the same shape from a different
    cause: the tool SPLITS AN INSTRUCTION'S LINE when a label comment falls inside it, emitting
    the leading bytes on one line and the trailing bytes plus the whole mnemonic on the next --
      2C5D 98
      ; A6
      2C5E 62 2C      ADC  $2C,#$62
    where the real instruction is "98 62 2C  ADC $2C,#$62" at 2C5D. All five are inside
    gradius3's uploaded sample data, so the alignment there is arbitrary anyway.

    The harness recognizes this class (a row whose address is inside an instruction we started
    earlier) and scores it against the containing instruction; 15 rows classified that way, of
    which the 8 above still differ in text and correctly land in the residue for a human to see.
    That is the right outcome -- these are real information about the code, not noise.

(B) EIGHT ROWS ARE ERRORS IN THE LISTINGS. We are right in all eight.

    SIX are ff3spc.dis failing to split the bit instructions' operand into its 3-bit index and
    13-bit address:
      090B EA 98 00   NOT1 $0098      should be  NOT1 $98.0
      0FBC CA 86 C0   MOV1 $C086,C    should be  MOV1 $86.6,C
      1134 EA 86 80   NOT1 $8086      should be  NOT1 $86.4
      121D AA A2 E0   MOV1 C,$E0A2    should be  MOV1 C,$A2.7
      1223 EA 4D E0   NOT1 $E04D      should be  NOT1 $4D.7
      1229 EA 4D E0   NOT1 $E04D      should be  NOT1 $4D.7
    It prints the raw 16-bit operand instead. INTERMITTENT, not systematic -- the SAME FILE gets
    it right elsewhere (1205 "MOV1 C,$00A2.7", 1286 "NOT1 $0076.7", 0C77 "MOV1 $0085.3,C"), and
    those correct ones use a bare ".7" while the tool's normal output elsewhere in the corpus is
    ".#7". Reading that as hand correction of raw tool output fits ff3 being the earliest and
    most hand-worked title; worth a question to the owner rather than a conclusion.

    ONE is a one-character typo, ff3spc.dis:1586:
      0E92 F0 7F      BEQ  $0E13      should be  BEQ $0F13    (0E94 + 0x7F)
    Checked the hypothesis that the tool mishandles the 0x7F sign boundary: it does NOT --
    fzerospc.dis:4984 "3035 30 7F  BMI $30B6" is correct, and it is the only other 7F-offset
    short branch in the corpus. E vs F, one character, almost certainly a hand edit.

    ONE is lemspc.dis:1377, in FF filler after the CPU-command jump table:
      1286 FF FF      OR $FF<d>,$FF<s>   -- FF is STOP, and the same file says STOP at 1288-128A

TWO LISTING ADDRESS-COLUMN SLIPS FOUND AS A SIDE EFFECT, both one byte, both inside data, so
neither can affect any instruction (the harness now only fails on a conflict that lands inside a
listing-declared instruction):
  ctspc.dis:3466   13-byte dump row at 1D87 runs to 1D93, where the next row also starts
  mariospc.dis:1747  a pad byte labelled 12F0 directly after a pointer that already ends there

THE COMMENT-CLASSIFICATION QUESTION THIS BEAD OPENED IS ANSWERED, AND THE ANSWER IS "IT DOES NOT
APPLY HERE". The frequency rule from the earlier comment was measured on the 65816 side
(som0*.dis), where the automated vocabulary repeats hundreds of times. On the SPC700 .dis files
there is NO automated comment vocabulary at all: the most-repeated comment text in any listing
occurs 10 times ("restart main loop" in sd3) and the rest of the top of every distribution is
3-7 occurrences of recurring hand idioms ("foreach voice", "next voice", "get next vbyte").
Nothing looks table-emitted. So on this side of the corpus, treat essentially every comment as
hand knowledge and drop the weighting scheme -- it was solving a problem these files do not
have. (It remains correct for the 65816 listings.)

SECOND ASSET HARVESTED: the code/data map. Each run also writes <title>-datamap.tsv --
contiguous data regions with the section heading that introduces each and the per-entry index
labels. This is exactly the information a fresh SPC import lacks. som, for instance:

  1418-1427   8 entries  dispatch table for CPU cmd FE subcommands   00..07
  1428-1483  46 entries  vcmd dispatch table (D2-FF)                 D2,D3,...,DD - set noise freq,...
  1484-14B1   6 entries  opcode length table                         D2-D7,D8-DF,E0-E7,...
  14B2-14F1  32 entries  table for CPU cmds 80-8F and F0-FF          80,81 - NOP,...
  14F2-150B  13 entries  pitch table                                 C,C#,D,...
  150C-152B   4 entries  filter coeffecients table
  152C-153A   1 entry    duration table
  153B-155A  16 entries  table for CPU cmds 10-1F
  155B-1597             vcmds for CPU cmds 10/11/12, shadow reg table

ff3's map is richer still (its labels carry the pointer targets and roles, e.g. "C4: 11D3 set
voice volume"). Nothing has been committed from the corpus itself -- no derived expectation
file, no harvested table map -- per this bead's licensing note; those TSVs are build output. If
any of it should become a committed fixture or a hint source, that is a decision to raise
separately.

WHAT IS NOT DONE / OPEN QUESTIONS FOR THE OWNER
 1. The six ff3 bit-operand rows: is the "raw $E04D" form the tool's output and the ".7" form
    your hand correction? That would date ff3's listing to an earlier tool version and is worth
    knowing before trusting any other ff3-specific oddity.
 2. ff2 and lufia were never in scope here (no *spc.dis). ff2/notes.txt in particular was
    flagged in an earlier comment as the most informative artifact in the corpus and is still
    unread by any agent.
 3. Whether the datamap harvest should become a committed artifact / disassembly-hint source.

comments.author: Chris Bongaarts
comments.text:
FF2 ADDED TO THE DIFFERENTIAL, AND IT CHANGES THE STORY. CORPUS IS NOW TEN LISTINGS: 31,404
INSTRUCTIONS, 254/256 OPCODES, 55 RESIDUAL DISAGREEMENTS, STILL NONE OF THEM OURS. Six of the
ten listings agree on every single instruction.

FIRST, THE ROM EXTRACTION, because ff2 had no .bin and its listing had never been checked
against anything. tools/spc700/extract-upload-blocks.py now walks the standard SNES upload
stream (word length, word target address, data; terminated by length 0 + execution address) out
of a ROM and writes it verbatim -- the same shape as the *spc.bin files already in the tree
(somspc.bin opens "98 13 00 02" = $1398 at $0200 and is exactly 4+$1398+4 bytes), or --image for
a flat 64K SPC memory image.

ff2's work.txt records "send blocks 04/8683 - 04/BBCF". THAT CHECKED OUT BEFORE THE ROM WAS EVEN
OPENED: the eight block lengths in notes.txt sum to $3529, plus 8 four-byte headers and the
4-byte terminator is $354D, and $8683 + $354D = $BBD0 -- exactly one past the stated end. The
extraction then reproduced all eight blocks in stream order with the starts and lengths
notes.txt gives, execution address $0800. AND THE INDEPENDENT CHECK: every byte of ff2spc.txt's
byte column matches the extracted image, 4,521 bytes agreeing and ZERO disagreeing. 4,521 is
exactly block 00's length ($11A9), so the listing covers the code block only -- not the seven
sample and directory-table blocks that ship with it.

The .bin is in scratchpad, not committed and not written into your tree; say where you want it
and it can be placed (snes/ff2/ff2spc.bin would match every other title's convention).

NOW THE FINDING, WHICH SUPERSEDES MY EARLIER "ONE-CHARACTER TYPO" READING OF ff3's BEQ.

THE TWO EARLIEST LISTINGS WERE PRODUCED BY AN EARLIER, BUGGIER VERSION OF THE SAME DISASSEMBLER,
AND THE CORPUS DATES THE FIXES. All 42 listing-error rows in the whole corpus are in ff2 (May
2000) and ff3 (Feb 2001). Nothing from March 2001 onward has a single one.

 1. FF2 REVERSES THE OPERAND ORDER OF EVERY dp,dp FORM -- 31 rows, the largest single class in
    the corpus. Its own <d>/<s> markers state the wrong claim outright:

      ff2  086B  69 7A 7B   CMP $7A<d>,$7B<s>     ours: CMP 0x7b,0x7a
      ff2  094D  09 8D 89   OR  $8D<d>,$89<s>     ours: OR  0x89,0x8d

    THE VECTOR SUITE SETTLES IT, since it is an oracle for which cell changes. Case "09 0000":
    instruction bytes 09 BF 09, initial ram[$09]=$94 and ram[$BF]=$95, final ram[$09]=$95 with
    $BF untouched. $94|$95 = $95. So the DESTINATION is the SECOND operand byte, which is what
    our spc700ops.sinc encodes (":OR dstaddr,srcaddr is op=0x09; srcaddr; dstaddr") and what we
    print. ff2 has it backwards.

    AND ff3 ALREADY HAS IT RIGHT: "0363 09 8F 24  OR $24<d>,$8F<s>" -- destination $24, the
    second byte. Same file family, same markers, opposite (correct) claim. So this was fixed
    between May 2000 and Feb 2001.

 2. FF3'S BIT-INSTRUCTION OPERAND SPLIT -- 6 rows, as reported before. YOU CONFIRMED (2026-08-18)
    that the disassembler did not handle those correctly and the correctly-split lines in that
    file are your hand corrections. That is now recorded in the human-research-todo Answered
    table and the item is retired.

 3. THE 0x7F BRANCH BUG IS SYSTEMATIC, NOT A TYPO. I WAS WRONG ABOUT THIS AND THE CORRECTION
    MATTERS, because "typo" invites reading other ff2/ff3 oddities as one-offs when they are not.

      ff3  0E92  F0 7F   BEQ $0E13    correct: $0F13   (0E94 + 0x7F)
      ff2  1890  10 7F   BPL $1811    correct: $1911   (1892 + 0x7F)

    Both exactly $100 low, in two independent files. The boundary is precisely at 0x7F: I checked
    every 2-byte relative branch in both listings, and every offset >= 0x80 is correctly negative
    while ff2's own "12B1 F0 76 BEQ $1329" (+0x76) and "1482 2F 78 BRA $14FC" (+0x78) are
    correct. So the sign test was written ">= 0x7F" instead of ">= 0x80". fzero (Aug 2001) gets
    0x7F right -- "3035 30 7F BMI $30B6" -- so this was fixed too, later than the dp,dp order.

 4. FF2 ALSO MIS-DECODES FOUR INDIVIDUAL OPCODES that no later listing gets wrong:
      5A -> "MOVW YA,dp"   (5A is CMPW YA,dp; MOVW YA,dp is BA)   2 rows
      3B -> "ROR dp+X"     (3B is ROL dp+X; ROR dp+X is 6B)       1 row
      BE -> "DAS YA"       (BE is DAS A)                          3 rows
      A7 -> "SBC A,[dp]"   (A7 is SBC A,[dp+X]; the +X is dropped) 1 row

PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCE FOR ANYONE USING THESE FILES: read an ff2- or ff3-only oddity as an
early-tool artifact FIRST, and do not spend effort reconciling one against a later listing or
against our output. The March-2001-and-later listings (som, sd3, ct, ff5, mario, gradius3,
fzero) have no listing errors at all in 27,000 instructions and can be leaned on much harder.

RESIDUE BREAKDOWN, ALL TEN LISTINGS (55 rows):
  ff2       31  dp,dp operand order reversed
  ff2        8  mis-decoded opcodes (5A/3B/BE/A7) + the 0x7F branch
  ff3        6  unsplit bit-instruction operand
  ff3        1  the 0x7F branch
  ff3        3  deliberate skip-op overlapping instruction streams (both decodes correct)
  gradius3   5  tool line-splitting inside its uploaded sample data (both decodes correct)
  lem        1  FF FF in filler decoded as OR dp,dp; FF is STOP, and the same file says so at 1288

HARVEST DECISION RECORDED (owner, 2026-08-18): the <title>-datamap.tsv code/data harvest STAYS
UNCOMMITTED for now -- in theory everything useful ends up in a game-specific yaml eventually
(grm-hb6 territory). It is regenerated by the tier on every run, so nothing is lost by not
committing it.

STILL OPEN: lufia has no *spc.dis and no notes, only lufia.smc / lufiadis.txt / lufia.idb -- out
of scope here and probably grm-w4w3's (the .idb inventory) rather than this bead's.

RE-RUN AT ANY TIME:

Worth doing after any data/languages/spc700*.sinc change that could move decode text, which the
