title: SPC700 DIV YA,X computes the wrong quotient, not just the wrong flags
description:
SPC700 DIV YA,X computes the wrong quotient, not just the wrong flags

Found during grm-c9d.3 increment 7 and deliberately NOT fixed there, because fixing it
properly is a different job from adding flags to a correct value.

THE VENDORED BODY DOES PLAIN TRUNCATING 16/8 DIVISION:

    local dividend:2 = YA;
    local divisor:2  = zext(X);
    local quotient:2 = dividend / divisor;
    ...
    A = quotient:1;  Y = remainder:1;

REAL HARDWARE DOES NOT. The SPC700 runs a quirky restoring-division algorithm that diverges
from plain division once the true quotient would overflow 8 bits. Measured against the
exhaustive vector suite:

    case 9E 0005:  Y=0xD1  A=0xAE  X=0x52
        expected:  A=0xBC  Y=0x76
        this body: A=0x8E  Y=0x32

Roughly a QUARTER of the sampled cases fall in the divergent range, so this is not an
edge case -- it is the common path for large dividends.

WHY FLAGS WERE NOT ADDED AT THE SAME TIME, which is the point of filing this separately: a
V/H formula was drafted from commonly cited documentation during increment 7 and then
REVERTED. With A and Y already wrong on the divergent cases, no flag formula can be validated
against those same cases -- the vectors cannot distinguish "your flags are wrong" from "your
quotient is wrong, so of course the flags disagree". Adding them would have produced
unfalsifiable code that looked finished, which is precisely the failure mode grm-c9d.2 exists
to prevent. DIV is therefore left flagless with an explanatory comment on the constructor.

ORDER OF WORK, and it matters:
 1. implement the real restoring-division algorithm so A and Y are right
 2. THEN derive V and H against the vectors, on top of a value that is actually correct

DIV's V flag is reportedly tied to quotient overflow and H to a nibble comparison, but treat
both as unverified until step 1 lands -- that is exactly the documentation this exercise has
already caught being wrong or incomplete several times (MUL sets N/Z from Y alone, not YA;
MOVW dp,YA genuinely sets no flags; H is an inverted borrow for subtraction).

UPSTREAMABLE (grm-c9d.6): yes, and cleanly -- it is self-contained to one constructor and
does not touch the ADDR8/ADDR16 structural work. Likely of real interest to SPCdra, since a
wrong quotient is a more serious defect than a missing flag.

Verify with: the exhaustive tier (bash tools/banktest/build-and-test.sh check spc700-vectors),
opcode 9E, currently failing. 1000 cases is ample to pin the algorithm's behaviour across the
whole divergent range.
close_reason: Exhaustive vector tier: 254 PASS / 0 FAIL / 2 N/A of 256; 253,970 of 254,000 applicable cases pass, remaining 30 are classified Ghidra decode-boundary artifacts. DIV YA,X now implements the real restoring-division algorithm with verified V/H. No known semantic defect remains.

title: Collect a corpus of extracted SPC700 upload images as reference and test data
description:
Collect a corpus of extracted SPC700 upload images as reference and test data

The project owner is collecting extracted SPC700 upload images from SNES games, for use as
real-ROM-tier test data and as reference targets for disassembly. This bead tracks the corpus
and the container format; it is a data/collection task, not a code change.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND "more test data": these files are GROUND TRUTH FOR grm-1.7.3's
extractor. docs/smc-survey.md:159 already rules that ROM-side extraction should parse the
boot-time IPL uploads whose $2140-43 handshake carries address+length+data records, and :171
that recovery must ACCUMULATE all transfers into one 64K SPC700 RAM image. An independently
produced extraction of the same game gives us something to diff our extractor's output
against, rather than only being able to check that it produced something plausible.

CONTAINER FORMAT, confirmed by parsing rather than taken on description (2026-08-17):

    repeat:
        u16  size      little endian
        u16  dest      little endian, destination address in SPC700 RAM
        u8[size] data
    until size == 0, where that final record's "dest" field is the ENTRY POINT.

This mirrors the transfer protocol rather than being an emulator save format -- note it is
NOT .spc (which is a 64K post-upload snapshot plus DSP state). It is the upload script.

FIRST SAMPLE: Z:/git/game-music-extraction/snes/som/somspc.bin (Secret of Mana), 5024 bytes,
dated 2001. Parses cleanly and exactly:

    block 0: size=5016 (0x1398)  dest=0x0200   covering 0x0200-0x1597
    terminator: size=0, entry=0x0200
    trailing bytes after terminator: 0

Consuming all 5024 bytes with nothing left over is a strong validity check on the format.

The payload is unambiguously real SPC700 driver code. Hand-decoded head:

    20        CLRP           ; direct page -> 0
    C0        DI
    CD FF     MOV X,#$FF
    BD        MOV SP,X       ; stack to $01FF
    E8 00     MOV A,#$00
    5D        MOV X,A
    AF        MOV (X)+,A     ; zero-fill loop
    C8 F0     CMP X,#$F0
    D0 FB     BNE -5

A textbook APU init. Incidentally a good validation of grm-c9d.3's work: MOV (X)+,A is one
of the implied-register forms that increment 4 had to teach the P fold, and CLRP as the very
first instruction is precisely why P cannot be modelled as a decode-time constant.

WHAT THIS SAMPLE DOES NOT COVER, and what to collect next: Secret of Mana uploads a SINGLE
block, so it does not exercise the multi-upload accumulation case that smc-survey.md:168-177
identifies as the norm ("a typical game runs the IPL multiple times to populate different
regions of the same SPC700 RAM"). A multi-block sample is worth more to us than another
single-block one. Also worth having: a game whose entry point is NOT the first block's
destination, since somspc.bin's entry (0x0200) coincides with its only block's address and so
cannot distinguish "entry" from "first destination" in any consumer we write.

OPEN QUESTIONS FOR THE OWNER, none blocking:
 * Is the format the owner's own convention from game-music-extraction, or a third-party
   container with a name? Affects whether we document it as "the GME upload format" or ours.
 * Are these committed anywhere durable, or reproduced by tooling from the ROM? Determines
   whether a test can pin one by hash the way the real-ROM tier does.

Related: grm-1.7.3 (SPC700 upload extraction), grm-c9d.4 (.spc loader -- note this format is
NOT .spc and would be a separate, simpler loader or import script), grm-c9d (epic).

comments.author: Chris Bongaarts
comments.text:
SAMPLE 2: Final Fantasy 3 (US) -- Z:/git/game-music-extraction/snes/ff3/ff3spc.bin
6079 bytes, dated 2001-02-22. Parses cleanly under the same container format:

    block 0: size=6071 (0x17B7)  dest=0x0200  covering 0x0200-0x19B6
    terminator: size=0, entry=0x0200
    trailing bytes: 0

Second file to consume its bytes exactly with nothing left over, which further confirms the
format reading is right and not a coincidence on one file.

BOTH SAMPLES ARE SQUARE/AKAO DRIVERS, so comparing them answers a question the epic cares
about -- is AKAO one binary we disassemble once, or a family? MEASURED: a family.

    common prefix: exactly 13 bytes, 0x0200-0x020C
    overall byte match across the 5016-byte overlap: 56 bytes, 1.1% -- i.e. noise
    first divergence: file offset 0x0D, SPC address 0x020D

The shared 13 bytes are the init:

    20        CLRP
    C0        DI
    CD FF     MOV X,#$FF
    BD        MOV SP,X
    E8 00     MOV A,#$00
    5D        MOV X,A
    AF        MOV (X)+,A
    C8 F0     CMP X,#$F0
    D0 FB     BNE -5

Immediately after, the two are STRUCTURALLY identical but not byte-identical -- FF3 inserts a
DECW $C6, and the following idiom is the same shape with a relocated call target:

    som: E8 00  8D 0C  3F 1B 06   MOV A,#0 ; MOV Y,#$0C ; CALL $061B
    ff3: E8 00  8D 0C  3F 48 06   MOV A,#0 ; MOV Y,#$0C ; CALL $0648

CONSEQUENCE FOR THE EPIC: a per-game disassembly is unavoidable -- there is no single AKAO
image to reverse once and reuse. But the shared idioms and identical call SHAPES mean the
transferable assets are recognizers, symbol naming conventions, and structural knowledge
(where the init ends, that a CALL follows a Y-register selector), not addresses. That is an
argument for investing in an analyzer/recognizer rather than a per-game symbol file, and it
is a much cheaper conclusion to reach from two files than from reverse-engineering one.

STILL NOT COVERED after two samples: both are SINGLE-BLOCK with entry == the only block's
destination, so neither exercises (a) the multi-upload accumulation case that
docs/smc-survey.md:168-177 calls the norm, nor (b) any consumer's ability to tell "entry
point" apart from "first destination". Both gaps still need a sample to close, and a
multi-block one remains the highest-value next addition.

comments.author: Chris Bongaarts
comments.text:
CORRECTION AND MAJOR FINDING 2026-08-17, from reading the extractor scripts (dumpspc.pl et al,
which sit beside each sample and name the ROM offset). This revises what I recorded earlier.

WHAT I GOT WRONG: I described the .bin container as "the format it is stored in", full stop.
Half right. The [len][addr][data] RECORDS are genuinely the ROM's own upload script, but the
TERMINATOR AND ENTRY POINT ARE SYNTHESIZED BY THE SCRIPTS. E.g. minidumpspc.pl:

    print OUT pack("v", length($buf)), $addr, $buf, pack("v", 0), $addr;

It reuses $addr as the trailing "entry". That fully explains why entry == first block's
destination in every sample -- I had flagged that coincidence as a gap in the corpus, and it
is not a property of the games at all. NO ENTRY POINT IS BEING RECOVERED FROM THE ROM in any
of these; do not build a consumer that trusts that field as an entry point.

THE MULTI-BLOCK EXAMPLE ALREADY EXISTS -- it is F-Zero, and it is why that directory has the
fzspc-*.bin files. fzero/dumpspc.pl is the only one of the four that LOOPS:

    seek IN, 0x008000 + 0x200, 0;
    for (;;) { read 4 bytes -> ($len,$addr); last unless $len > 0; read $len; write piece }

producing five pieces, in upload order:
    0: 0x0500, 624 bytes      3: 0xa080, 10381 bytes
    1: 0x3cc0, 422 bytes      4: 0x07fe, 1 byte
    2: 0x0800, 13306 bytes
Piece 4 being a SINGLE BYTE at 0x07FE is almost certainly a trigger/start write rather than
payload -- exactly the kind of thing an accumulating recovery model must not mistake for code.
fzerospc.bin is NOT the whole upload: minidumpspc.pl re-reads only the 0x0800 chunk from
0x00841e and wraps it. So the corpus already covers the multi-piece case; it was just filed
under a different naming scheme.

THE ROM FORMAT IS NOT UNIFORM ACROSS GAMES, and this is the finding that matters for
grm-1.7.3:

  game   ROM location (script)                          record shape
  ----   --------------------------------------------   -----------------------------------
  fzero  fzero.smc    0x008000 + 0x200 hdr               LOOP of [u16 len][u16 addr][data],
                                                         terminated by len==0. Real block list.
  lem    lemmings.smc 8*0x8000 + (0xe7d7-0x8000)         [u16 len][u16 addr][data], single
                      = 0x467D7, and NOTE no +0x200      record (script does not loop)
  som    som1.smc     0x030748 + 0x200 hdr               [u16 len][data] -- NO ADDRESS FIELD.
                                                         Script hardcodes dest 0x0200.
  ff3    f_fan3.fig   0x05070e + 0x200 hdr               [u16 len][data] -- NO ADDRESS FIELD.
                                                         Script hardcodes dest 0x0200.

So on the two AKAO titles the DESTINATION IS NOT IN THE DATA AT ALL -- it lives in the 65816
uploader code, and the human extracting it supplied 0x0200 by hand. A static parser cannot
recover it from the block stream because it is not there.

THIS IS DIRECT EVIDENCE FOR docs/smc-survey.md's HYBRID RULING, and sharpens it. The survey
proposed a static tier ("the $2140-43 handshake carries documented address+length+data
records") plus a generic emulation tier. These four samples show the split is not a
convenience but a necessity: F-Zero's static block list is parseable with no emulation at all,
while SoM and FF3 need the uploader's CODE to know where the bytes go. Any plan that assumes
one universal ROM layout will work on F-Zero and silently produce address-less blobs on the
Square titles.

Also worth noting the SMC header inconsistency (three files need +0x200, lemmings.smc does
not) -- a real extractor must detect the 512-byte copier header rather than assume it.

AKAO UPLOADS ARE CODE ONLY. Per the owner: AKAO drivers stream instrument samples on demand
as songs play, so these extracts contain no BRR sample data. That explains the size gap --
som 5016 / ff3 6071 bytes versus F-Zero's 13306+10381 across two large pieces, where the
non-AKAO driver ships its samples up front. Consequence for us: an AKAO extract is almost
pure code, which makes it the BETTER disassembly target, while an F-Zero-style image needs
code/data separation before it is useful.

SECOND ASSET FOUND, and it may be worth as much as the binaries: nine ANNOTATED REFERENCE
DISASSEMBLIES exist in the corpus -- ct, ff3, ff5, fzero, gradius3, lem, mario, sd3, som
(*spc.dis, 32K-204K each). They carry addresses, bytes, mnemonics AND hand comments:

    0200 20         CLRP               ; dpage = 0
    0201 C0         DI                 ; interrupts off
    0202 CD FF      MOV     X,#$FF
    0204 BD         MOV     SP,X       ; SP = $(01)FF
    ...
    020B D0 FB      BNE     $0208      ; zero $00-$EF

My independent hand-decode of somspc.bin matched somspc.dis line for line. These are usable
two ways: as GROUND TRUTH for grm-c9d.3's disassembly (diff our listing against a known-good
one over thousands of real instructions, far beyond what Spc700LanguageTest's 8 encodings
pin), and as a symbol/comment source for AKAO analysis. Worth its own bead if we act on it.

CORPUS STATUS: four parsed samples (som, ff3, fzero, lem), all consuming their bytes exactly;
multi-piece case COVERED by fzero's five pieces; entry-point recovery still uncovered and now
known to be uncoverable from these files by construction.

comments.author: Chris Bongaarts
comments.text:
THE MULTI-BLOCK EXAMPLE EXISTS, AND IT IS FF2 -- documented rather than extracted, in
Z:/git/game-music-extraction/snes/ff2/notes.txt. This closes the gap I flagged twice above
(both earlier samples being single-block with entry == the only destination).

    Block 00: start $0800 length $11A9   code
    Block 01: start $FF00 length $0020   data?
    Block 02: start $1E00 length $0020   dir table for $CA70 (default)
    Block 03: start $CA70 length $0590   samples
    Block 04: start $F900 length $0400   samples
    Block 05: start $1D00 length $0040   dir table for $F900
    Block 06: start $B300 length $1770   samples
    Block 07: start $FD00 length $0200   dir table for $B300
    Execution Address: $0800

EIGHT blocks, and note EXECUTION ADDRESS IS RECORDED AS ITS OWN FIELD. It happens to equal
block 00's start here, so this still does not distinguish "entry" from "first destination" by
value -- but it establishes that the uploader carries it as a distinct datum, which the
synthesized .bin containers had left ambiguous (they fabricate the entry by reusing the first
block's address; see the correction above).

There is NO ff2spc.bin. The blocks were never dumped to the container format -- what exists is
notes.txt plus ff2spc.txt (65 KB), a disassembly whose own header shows the blocks being
loaded by the owner's tool ("SPC700 Disassembler v0.1"), assembling the 64K image from all
eight pieces. That is itself the accumulate-into-one-RAM-image model docs/smc-survey.md:171
specifies, implemented by hand in 2000.

CORRECTS AN OVERGENERALIZATION OF MINE. I recorded that "AKAO drivers stream instrument
samples on demand, so these extracts are code only". FF2 IS AKAO AND UPLOADS ITS SAMPLES UP
FRONT -- three sample blocks (CA70, F900, B300) plus three BRR directory tables. So the
streaming behaviour belongs to the LATER AKAO versions (SoM, FF3), not to AKAO as such. The
earlier claim should be read as version-specific, and any recognizer must not assume an AKAO
upload is pure code.

STRUCTURE WORTH KEEPING: the block roles here (code / sample data / BRR directory table) are a
useful taxonomy for what an SPC700 upload contains, and the notes even record which directory
serves which sample region. A loader or analyzer that can label uploaded regions by role would
be far more useful than one that dumps 64K undifferentiated -- and this is a worked example to
design against.

FF2 IS THE ORIGIN OF THE WHOLE CORPUS, per the owner: he worked FF2 first, FF3 second, the
rest after. The filesystem agrees and pushes the start date back nearly a year before anything
previously recorded -- ff2's files run from MAY 2000, versus ff3's Feb 2001. It also holds 32
per-bank 65816 listings (ffdis00.txt .. ffdis1F.txt, ~460-510 KB each, ~15 MB total), plus
notes.txt (30 KB) and work.txt (22 KB).

AND THE STRONGEST FORM OF THE "ABSENCE MEANS NOT EXAMINED" CAVEAT: per the owner, MOST OF THE
FF2 SPC ANALYSIS WAS DONE BY HAND ON A PAPER PRINTOUT. The most-analyzed title in the corpus
is therefore among the least annotated on disk -- ff2spc.txt has 132 commented lines out of
2224. Any ranking by comment density would put the origin title near the bottom, which would
be exactly wrong. notes.txt is where that understanding actually landed, so READ THE NOTES
FILES, not just the listings.

Also present and previously unlisted: lufia/, containing lufia.idb -- an IDA Pro database, a
different toolchain from everything else here. Reading it would need IDA or an .idb parser;
note it exists rather than assuming the corpus is uniform.

comments.author: Chris Bongaarts
comments.text:
CORRECTION on AKAO sample handling, and it carries a design consequence for the recovery model.

I have now had two goes at this and both were too coarse. Precisely, per the owner:

  AKAO uploads samples AS NEEDED FOR BACKGROUND MUSIC. There are ALSO sound-effect samples and
  the like which are PERMANENTLY RESIDENT.

So it is not "AKAO extracts are code only" (my first version), nor "early AKAO uploads samples
up front while later AKAO streams" (my second, from FF2's eight blocks). EVERY AKAO version
does BOTH: a resident set goes up in the initial upload, and BGM sample data is streamed per
song thereafter. What differs between titles is HOW MUCH is resident, not whether streaming
happens.

That is consistent with everything measured: FF2's initial upload carries three sample blocks
plus three BRR directory tables (~9.5 KB of sample data) because its resident set is large,
while SoM's 5016 bytes and FF3's 6071 are essentially pure code with a smaller or separately
loaded resident set. Same architecture, different split.

THE CONSEQUENCE FOR grm-1.7.3's RECOVERY MODEL, which is the reason this is worth writing down
rather than being trivia: docs/smc-survey.md:171 rules that recovery should ACCUMULATE ALL IPL
TRANSFERS INTO ONE 64K SPC700 RAM IMAGE, on the model of an .spc snapshot. That is right for
CODE and for the resident set, but it is NOT a complete description of the machine's life --
BGM sample regions are OVERWRITTEN REPEATEDLY AT RUNTIME, once per song change. An accumulated
image is therefore a POINT IN TIME, and some address ranges are legitimately multi-valued over
the program's execution.

Practical implications, none of which invalidate the accumulate model but all of which qualify it:
 * A region that later gets streamed over is not "the" contents of that address -- labelling it
   as settled data would be wrong. It is one occupant of a slot, which is precisely the banked-
   occupant situation this project already models with overlays elsewhere.
 * Code and the resident set are stable and safe to treat as the program; streamed BGM sample
   regions are transient buffers and are better modelled as such (an uninitialized or
   overlay-style region) than as recovered bytes.
 * FF2's notes.txt gives the taxonomy to key on -- each block is tagged code / samples / BRR
   directory table, and the directory tables say which sample region they serve. A recovery
   pass that preserved those roles would be able to make exactly this distinction, rather than
   producing 64K of undifferentiated bytes.
 * The BRR directory tables are the structural hook: a dir table pointing into a region is
   evidence that region is sample data rather than code, available statically.

Do not read this as an argument to change the accumulate model. It is an argument to record
PROVENANCE AND ROLE per region while accumulating, so a later consumer can tell "this is the
driver" from "this is whatever song happened to be loaded when the snapshot was taken".

comments.author: Chris Bongaarts
comments.text:
SCOPING NOTE on the preceding comment: THE ON-DEMAND SAMPLE LOADING IS SPECIFIC TO THE AKAO
FAMILY. Per the owner, other drivers may have approached sample loading entirely differently,
and he does not recall how most of them handled it.

So the corrected model above -- resident set up front, BGM samples streamed per song -- is a
statement about AKAO (Square: FF2, FF3, FF5, SoM, SD3, Chrono Trigger), NOT about SNES audio
drivers generally. Do not carry it over to F-Zero, Lemmings, Gradius III, Super Mario World or
anything else in the corpus.

WHAT THAT MEANS FOR THE RECOVERY MODEL: the design has to tolerate BOTH ends of a spectrum
without knowing in advance which a title sits at.

  * A FULLY-RESIDENT driver uploads everything once and never streams. For those, the
    accumulate-into-one-64K-image model is COMPLETE, not a point in time, and every recovered
    region is stable. F-Zero looks like a plausible candidate -- its five blocks total ~24 KB
    including two large ones, which is a lot to be pure code -- but that is an inference from
    size, NOT a measurement, and it should be checked rather than assumed.
  * An AKAO-style driver streams, so parts of the image are transient. Accumulation is a
    snapshot.

The practical upshot is that "is this region stable code/data or a transient buffer?" is a
PER-DRIVER question with no universal answer, and nothing in the ROM header or the upload
format announces it. Two honest options for a recovery pass: recover the accumulated image and
label regions by evidence (a BRR directory table pointing into a region is static evidence it
is sample data, per the previous comment), or emulate far enough to observe whether a region
is rewritten. Do not build in an assumption either way.

AND DO NOT SPEND AGENT TOKENS RECONSTRUCTING THIS FROM THE ROMS. Determining how Lemmings or
Gradius III handled sample loading is hand reverse-engineering of a specific driver -- the
class of work CLAUDE.md designates as cheaper for a human with a disassembler than for an
agent running build/measure cycles. If it becomes load-bearing for a design decision, ASK,
and note that the owner's own recollection has already been offered and does not cover it.

comments.author: Chris Bongaarts
comments.text:
WHERE AKAO's SAMPLE MEMORY MANAGEMENT ACTUALLY LIVES: THE 65816 SIDE, NOT THE SPC700.

Per the owner (2026-08-17), for the AKAO family at least: the song format carries information
about which samples a song needs. The 65816 uploads those samples AND writes the BRR directory
entries that map them to the instrument slots the song format references. The SPC700 driver
then simply knows that to play instrument N it plays sample M -- the indirection is already
resolved for it.

THIS CHANGES WHERE THE INTERESTING CODE IS, and it is close to the opposite of what an
SPC700-first approach would assume:

 * An SPC700-only analysis WILL NOT FIND SAMPLE MANAGEMENT. There is nothing to find there --
   the driver reads a directory someone else populated and writes DSP registers. All the
   allocation, residency and mapping logic is ROM-side.
 * THE BRR DIRECTORY IN SPC RAM HAS NO WRITER VISIBLE IN THE SPC IMAGE. A static analysis of
   an uploaded image will see a table that nothing in that image ever writes. That is not a
   gap in the analysis -- its provenance is genuinely cross-processor. An analyzer should say
   so rather than leaving it as an unexplained data region.
 * grm-1.7.3's cross-processor extraction therefore matters twice over: the ROM side holds
   both the song->sample manifest and the code that builds the mapping. Recovering only the
   SPC700 image recovers the player, not the thing that decides what it plays.

CORRECTION TO MY EARLIER CLAIM, which was too strong. I wrote that "a BRR directory table
pointing into a region is static evidence that region is sample data rather than code,
available statically". That holds ONLY for directories present in the uploaded image -- i.e.
the RESIDENT set, like FF2's blocks 02/05/07 which are uploaded as dir tables alongside their
sample blocks. For STREAMED BGM samples the directory entries are written at runtime by the
65816 and are NOT in the upload at all, so the static hook simply does not exist for them. The
two facts fit together: resident samples ship with their directories, streamed ones get theirs
written later.

USEFUL STRUCTURE, for whenever this gets built:
 * A BRR directory entry is 4 bytes -- two 16-bit pointers, sample start and loop point.
 * The directory's base address is held in the DSP's DIR register, so the table's location is
   discoverable from a DSP register write rather than having to be guessed.
 * Instrument slot -> sample index is the mapping the 65816 writes; the song data references
   instrument slots, so reading song data without that mapping gives you slot numbers with no
   meaning attached.

SCOPE, AGAIN: this is an AKAO-family statement. Other drivers may divide the work between the
two processors completely differently, and the owner does not recall how most of them did it
(see the preceding scoping comment). Do not assume ROM-side sample management for anything
outside AKAO without checking, and treat "which side manages samples" as a per-driver question.

comments.author: Chris Bongaarts
comments.text:
CORRECTION to the preceding comment, which over-claimed. I wrote that "the 65816 uploads those
samples AND writes the BRR directory entries", and then built an analyzer expectation on top
of it ("the BRR directory has no writer visible in the SPC image"). That second step is NOT
established. Per the owner, it has been too long to recall whether the SPC-side driver
calculates the directory itself or the 65816 sends it as a chunk of data. Either is possible.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY KNOWN, separated by confidence:

CERTAIN:
 * The SPC700's role in sample management is to RECEIVE the samples from the 65816. The
   allocation decision -- which samples a song needs -- is made ROM-side.
 * THE 65816 RUNS THE SHOW AND THE SPC700 ACTS IN A "SLAVE" MODE. This is the durable
   architectural point, and unlike the sample-residency detail IT IS TYPICAL OF MOST SNES
   GAMES, not an AKAO peculiarity. It is the one generalization in this whole thread that the
   owner has stated broadly rather than scoped to a driver family.

LIKELY:
 * AKAO uses its own custom signalling protocol for these runtime transfers, but the upload
   MECHANISM is thought to be nearly the same as the boot-time IPL process. If so, a runtime
   sample upload looks structurally like an IPL upload, which is directly useful to
   grm-1.7.3: the same recognizer may serve both, and the accumulate-all-transfers model
   would naturally pick up runtime sample loads as well as the boot image.

UNKNOWN, and to be treated as an open question rather than filled in by inference:
 * Whether the BRR directory is computed by the SPC700 driver or sent by the 65816 as data.
   MY PREVIOUS COMMENT ASSERTED THE LATTER; that assertion should be disregarded.
 * Consequently the analyzer expectation I derived from it -- "a directory table with no
   writer in the SPC image is normal and cross-processor" -- is ALSO not established. It may
   be true, or the driver may build the table itself and the writer will be right there.
   Do not encode either as an assumption; if it matters, it is answerable by looking at one
   driver's code, which is a small, well-defined hand task rather than a design premise.

WHY THE MASTER/SLAVE POINT IS THE ONE TO BUILD ON: it says the SPC700 image is, on its own, an
incomplete artifact for almost any SNES title -- it is the subordinate half of a two-processor
system whose decisions are made elsewhere. That is an argument for grm-1.7.3's cross-processor
framing generally, independent of AKAO, and it does not depend on any of the uncertain details
above. It also sets expectations for what SPC700 decompilation can deliver: a faithful player,
with the "why" living in the ROM.

comments.author: Chris Bongaarts
comments.text:
THIRD ASSET IN THE CORPUS: THE CROSS-PROCESSOR COMMAND PROTOCOL, DOCUMENTED ON BOTH SIDES.

Per the owner (2026-08-17), at least a couple of the disassemblies carry comments where he
worked out the communication between the two processors -- "I'm sending song data", "play this
song", "set this variable used by the sequence interpreter", "enable the drum track because
Mario is on Yoshi". Notes exist on BOTH the SPC and 65816 sides in those cases, and at minimum
THE CODE AREAS ARE MECHANICALLY LOCATABLE: the IO register accesses on each side.

THE TWO SIDES OF ONE PORT PAIR:
  65816 side: $2140-$2143
  SPC700 side: $00F4-$00F7 (direct page)
Same four physical registers seen from opposite ends. The owner's own comment on ff3spc.dis
line 09E1 makes the link explicit -- "MOV X,$F4  ; check 2140" -- which is exactly the
cross-reference an analyzer would need to relate the two Programs.

MEASURED, SPC SIDE (direct-page $F4-$F7 only; an earlier count of mine was inflated by
matching absolute addresses like $F600+X, which are ordinary memory, not ports):

    sd3   113 refs,  4 commented        g3      5 refs, 0 commented
    ct     87 refs,  0 commented        fzero   2 refs, 0 commented
    ff3    78 refs, 15 commented        lem     0 refs, 0 commented
    som    60 refs, 13 commented        mario   0 refs, 0 commented
    ff5    49 refs,  5 commented

65816 side, from the earlier scan of $2140-43 references: som03 107, lem08 87, f3-05 85,
fzero00 17. The bank with ~100 references is the driver/uploader bank in every title.

RICHEST PROTOCOL DOCUMENTATION IS ff3 AND som, on both sides -- ff3 15 commented SPC-side port
lines and 85 on the 65816 side (f3-05); som 13 and 107 (som03). Those two are where the
protocol was actually worked out. Samples of the SPC-side comments:

    02A4 DA F6   MOVW $F6,YA     ; write $DD and $52 or $AD to APU2/3
    02AA DA F4   MOVW $F4,YA     ; write #$00 and $7B to APU0/1
    09E1 F8 F4   MOV  X,$F4      ; check 2140
    (section header)             ; process CPU cmd $F4

AN OPEN QUESTION, NOT A CONCLUSION: lem and mario show ZERO direct-page port references in
their SPC listings, and fzero/g3 show 2 and 5. A working driver must communicate somehow, so
the plausible explanations are (a) those listings cover only part of the image, (b) those
drivers use a different notation the grep missed, or (c) they genuinely poll differently.
Do not infer "these drivers don't use the ports". Given the repeated lesson in this corpus
that measurable artifacts under-determine the explanation, this is a question for the owner or
for reading one of those listings, not something to settle by more grepping.

WHY THIS MATTERS BEYOND ARCHAEOLOGY: the protocol IS the interface between the two Programs
that grm-1.7.3 will produce. Recovering an SPC700 image gives a player whose inputs are
opaque command bytes; the protocol comments say what those bytes MEAN. Concretely useful for:
 * naming the command dispatch table on the SPC side (ff3 has an explicit "process CPU cmd $F4"
   section, and the FF2 notes.txt records a full dispatch map of command -> handler address)
 * annotating the 65816 side's writes with their intent
 * giving a future analyzer a target: a $2140-43 write cluster on one side and a $F4-$F7 read
   dispatch on the other are two halves of one protocol, and relating them across Programs is
   exactly the cross-processor reference problem this project already thinks about for banking.

Consistent with the master/slave architecture recorded on grm-1.7.3: the 65816 issues commands
and the SPC obeys, so the command vocabulary is the SPC driver's real API.

comments.author: Chris Bongaarts
comments.text:
lufia/lufia.idb IS READABLE WITHOUT IDA -- reclassified from judgment call to agent work.

Two open-source pure-Python .idb parsers, both permissively licensed and compatible with this
project's Apache-2.0 (owner-supplied, verified 2026-08-17):

  williballenthin/python-idb   Apache-2.0   489 stars   ARCHIVED May 2025
      "Pure Python parser and analyzer for IDA Pro database files (.idb)."
  nlitsme/idbutil              MIT          164 stars   active, last push Nov 2023
      "Library and tool for reading IDApro databases."

ARCHIVED IS ACCEPTABLE HERE, unlike the caution applied to SingleStepTests' archived parent
repo, and the distinction is worth stating: this is a ONE-OFF READ of a local file, not a
dependency the project carries or a data source it re-syncs from. Nothing gets vendored, and
if the tool breaks we simply stop using it. Prefer whichever parses the file; try idbutil first
on maintenance grounds, fall back to python-idb.

WHY IT MAY BE THE RICHEST ITEM IN THE CORPUS. Every other annotated artifact here is flat text
-- .dis listings with an optional trailing comment per line. An .idb is a STRUCTURED DATABASE
and can carry things the text files structurally cannot:
  * named functions and labels, with boundaries
  * data type definitions and applied types (structs over tables, arrays)
  * repeatable comments, function comments, and comments anchored to addresses
  * segment/bank layout as the analyst configured it
  * cross-references the analyst confirmed
If the Lufia work was done in IDA rather than the homebrew disassembler, its annotations may be
both more complete and more machine-readable than anything in the nine .dis files -- and it is
the only title in the corpus in that format.

WHAT TO DO WHEN IT IS WANTED (small, bounded):
 1. pip install one of the two into a scratch venv; do NOT add either to this repo's build.
 2. Dump an inventory: segments, function count, named (non-auto) functions, comment count,
    defined data items with types.
 3. Report what classes of annotation exist and how much -- the point of the first pass is to
    decide whether a second pass is worth it, not to extract everything.
 4. Only then consider whether any of it should feed grm-uy9s (disassembly comparison) or
    grm-9nxj (SNES machine target -- an analyst-configured bank layout is directly relevant to
    LoROM/HiROM mapping).

CAVEATS to carry in: the same "not an oracle" framing as the .dis files applies -- IDA's
autoanalysis is not ground truth either, and the ANNOTATIONS are the asset, not the
disassembly. And Lufia is not a music-extraction title in the way the others are, so check
what the database was actually for before assuming it is about the audio driver.

comments.author: Chris Bongaarts
comments.text:
LUFIA CONTEXT AND DEFERRAL, per the owner 2026-08-17: Lufia was a LOWER-TIER music-extraction
title -- still music work, but not high priority, so there is considerably less effort behind
it than the AKAO titles or F-Zero. That tempers the "possibly the richest artifact in the
corpus" framing in my earlier comment: the FORMAT is richer (a structured database rather than
flat text), but the CONTENT behind it is thinner. Both can be true, and the format advantage
does not compensate for less work having gone in.

DEFERRED BY THE OWNER: do not run the .idb inventory yet -- that is for a future session. The
tooling note stands (python-idb / idbutil, both permissive, no IDA needed) so whoever picks it
up does not re-derive it, but nobody should spend tokens on the extraction now.

Expectations to set for whenever it happens: expect fewer named functions and comments than
ff3/som/ct carry, and check what the database was actually for before assuming it covers the
audio driver. A thin .idb is still worth twenty minutes for its segment/bank layout alone --
that is analyst-configured and bears on grm-9nxj -- but it should not be approached as a
comparable peer to the annotated .dis listings.

title: Two fallthrough wrappers into one bank-switch helper: only one is admitted, and which one is not deterministic
description:
MEASURED 2026-08-16 while building the grm-pfp skip-idiom fixture (nesskiptest.nes), on a
SYNTHETIC image, which is what makes it worth a bead of its own: no ROM idiosyncrasy is involved
and the whole program is nine instructions of relevant code.

THE SHAPE. Two fallthrough wrappers (grm-2dr's shape) into ONE bank-switch helper:

    C150  A9 02      LDA #$02      ; wrapper 1 -- the visible entry of a BIT-skip
    C157  2C A9 01   BIT $01A9     ; carrier, hiding LDA #$01 at C158
    C158  A9 01      LDA #$01      ; wrapper 2 -- the hidden entry, recovered by
                                   ;   ghidra_scripts/FixSkipInstructions.java
    C15A  AA         TAX           ; the SHARED TAIL, its own function: the latch
    C15B  9D D0 FF   STA $FFD0,X
    C15E  60         RTS

Both wrappers fall through into the same helper with a different constant in A. RESET calls both
(JSR $C150 and JSR $C158).

*** WHAT HAPPENS: EXACTLY ONE OF THE TWO CALL SITES RESOLVES, AND WHICH ONE IS NOT STABLE. ***
Only one wrapper is admitted. In the runs observed the OFFCUT entry usually won, leaving
JSR $C150 with no annotation at all -- and adding an UNRELATED probe call site elsewhere in the
image flipped which one won, on otherwise identical bytes. That last part is the finding: the
outcome depends on something other than the code being analyzed.

WHY THIS IS NOT THE SKIP SCRIPT'S DOING. The script's only effect here is that C158 exists at
all. Once it does, this is an ordinary two-wrappers-one-helper question that any image could pose
without a skip carrier anywhere in it -- a jump table with two entries that load different
constants and fall into a shared routine is the same shape. The skip idiom just makes it easy to
construct, because a carrier is BY CONSTRUCTION two paths through one instruction stream.

SUSPECTED RELATIVE, WORTH CHECKING BEFORE DESIGNING ANYTHING: grm-g73 (megaman realrom dump
bistable run-to-run) and grm-4nr (ff1, same but larger). Those are both "identical input, different
output between runs" on titles with helpers, which is the same signature as the flip observed
here. If wrapper admission is order-dependent on something like iteration order over a HashMap or
over the function manager, that would explain a run-to-run flap without any analyzer change. This
is a HYPOTHESIS, not a measurement -- but it is cheap to test against a synthetic image, which
neither of those beads has.

WORKAROUND USED IN THE FIXTURE, so it is not mistaken for a passing test of this behaviour:
nesskiptest gives its VISIBLE entry a switch of its own (STA $FFD2 at C152) so that entry is not
a wrapper at all. Both call sites then resolve deterministically and the fixture's criteria stay
about the REPAIR. The two-wrapper case is deliberately NOT asserted there.

THE HONEST STATEMENT OF THE LIMITATION, which may be the resolution rather than a bug to fix: a
path-insensitive helper summary has exactly one answer to give, and two wrappers passing different
constants is two answers. Admitting one arbitrarily is worse than either alternative -- declining
both (with a warning naming the ambiguity) or making the summary per-wrapper. Whichever is
chosen, the nondeterminism is a defect independent of the modelling question: the same bytes must
produce the same answer.

comments.author: Chris Bongaarts
comments.text:
2026-08-22 MEASURED: the flip does NOT reproduce on this machine at Ghidra 12.1.3, and a
prerequisite for ever asserting it headlessly turns out to be missing. Two findings, then an
open decision.

FINDING 1 -- SITE B IS ALREADY THE CONTESTED SHAPE, AND ITS GEOMETRY IS STABLE.
This bead describes site A ($C150 visible / $C158 offcut / $C15A Latch A), which mknesbanktest's
make_prg_skip took out of the contest by giving the visible entry its own switch at $C152. But
SITE B was never given that workaround and is the same two-wrappers-one-helper shape:

    C170  A9 02      LDA #$02      wrapper 1, visible entry
    C172  2C A9 01   BIT $01A9     carrier, hides LDA #$01 at C173
    C173  A9 01      LDA #$01      wrapper 2, offcut entry (created by FixSkipInstructions)
    C175  AA         TAX           Latch B, the shared tail / helper
    C176  9D D0 FF   STA $FFD0,X
    C179  60         RTS

So the contest is observable in the existing fixture with no image edit. Measured over SIX fresh
headless imports, via a throwaway -postScript that dumped getFunctionContaining/body at each
address (script since deleted; not committed):

    c170 -> FUN_c170  body [c170,c172]      c150 -> FUN_c150  body [c150,c157]
    c172 -> FUN_c170  body [c170,c172]      c157 -> FUN_c150  body [c150,c157]
    c173 -> FUN_c173  body [c173,c174]      c158 -> FUN_c158  body [c158,c159]
    c174 -> FUN_c173  body [c173,c174]      c15a -> FUN_c15a  body [c15a,c15e]
    c175 -> FUN_c175  body [c175,c179]

BYTE-IDENTICAL IN ALL SIX RUNS. The contested byte is $C174 (= helperEntry.previous() for
FUN_c175), and FUN_c173 owns it every time; FUN_c170's body stops at $C172 every time. Since
findPassThroughWrappers' only candidate lookup is getFunctionContaining(entry.previous()), and
Ghidra bodies cannot overlap so at most one function can ever own that byte, a stable geometry
means a stable admission. Site A is likewise stable, as expected.

This does NOT prove the 2026-08-16 observation was wrong. It was made on 12.1.2, on a
pre-workaround fixture shape, and the plausible race -- which function Ghidra's own initial-import
auto-analysis creates first, before FixSkipInstructions runs at all -- was not probed here.
FixSkipInstructions' own createFunction runs sequentially in a single-threaded postScript, which
is the likely reason the post-repair geometry is reproducible.

FINDING 2, THE BLOCKER -- THE ANALYZER'S HELPER-SET LOG IS INVISIBLE HEADLESSLY.
BoardBankAnalyzer.java:291 logs the sorted helper-function names via log.appendMsg(). That goes
into a ghidra.app.util.importer.MessageLog, which only reaches the console when something calls
MessageLog.write(). Verified two ways at 12.1.3:

  - Source: the only non-test consumer of AutoAnalysisManager.getMessageLog() is
    AutoAnalysisPlugin (GUI; Window > Analysis Messages). HeadlessAnalyzer never reads it.
    AnalysisScheduler only passes it into AnalysisTask.
  - Empirically: ran neswrappertest.nes (a fixture with live wrapper/helper functions) through
    analyzeHeadless and grepped the whole log for "helper" -- the line never appears.

Note this is the ANALYZER MessageLog, and does not contradict the loader-side convention in
CLAUDE.md ("assert on log content, never exit status") -- the IMPORTER writes its log; the
analysis manager does not.

CONSEQUENCE: there is currently NO WAY for a banktest criterion to assert which wrappers were
admitted. Site B confirms this from the other side -- nothing in the image references $C173
(deliberate; mknesbanktest.py:826-828), so the site-B admission outcome produces no comment and
no warning either way. The two comments the fixture does emit come from direct JSRs:
    COMMENT c00c bank -> 2 (bank=2) via FUN_c170
    COMMENT c019 bank -> 0 (bank=0) via FUN_c175

DISCRIMINATOR FOR ANY FUTURE FIX, if this is picked up again: getFunctionContaining(0xc174) right
after the FixSkipInstructions postScript. FUN_c173 = current/expected; FUN_c170, or any function
whose body swallows c174, = the bug reproduced.

ALSO WORTH RECORDING: the suspected shared cause with grm-g73 / grm-4nr now looks UNLIKELY.
Those move refs.intoOverlay and instrs.inOverlay in OPPOSITE directions -- raw Ghidra disassembly
and reference counts -- which is Ghidra's own analysis scheduling, not our helper bookkeeping.
Different phenomenon that happens to share the "same bytes, different output" signature.

comments.author: Chris Bongaarts
comments.text:
2026-08-22 STATUS, at the owner's direction: DOWNGRADED P2 -> P3, unclaimed, and blocked on
grm-6jfp. NOT closed, and NOT fixed -- "does not reproduce at 12.1.3 with the current fixture
geometry" is a weaker claim than "no longer a bug", and the difference is exactly what cannot be
checked right now.

Why blocked rather than open: the admission outcome this bead is about is invisible to every
headless probe (grm-6jfp), so no criterion can pin it and no fix can be validated in the test
tier. Two things unblock it, either one sufficient:

  1. grm-6jfp lands, making the helper set observable headlessly, or
  2. the owner reads Window > Analysis Messages in the GUI for nesskiptest site B and reports
     which of FUN_c170 / FUN_c173 the analyzer names. Filed as an item in section 1 of
     docs/human-research-todo.md.

Do not re-run the six-import geometry measurement; it is recorded in the previous comment and was
stable. The open question is admission, not geometry.

title: E2E gap: no fixture reaches a PARTIALLY-known bank field, the state grm-v6o fixes
description:
Found while fixing grm-v6o (the `!= 0` vs `== positionedMask()` bank-knowledge predicate).

## The coverage gap

`nesmmc1overridetest` exercises only the ENDPOINTS of the knowledge lattice:

- O3/O4: prg_bank fully UNKNOWN -> override fires, tagged `[user override]` -> W8000_M3_B5
- O5/O6: prg_bank fully KNOWN (all 5 bits) -> flow wins over override -> W8000_M3_B3

It never reaches the INTERIOR -- a partially-known multi-bit bank field -- which is
precisely the state grm-v6o was about. That is why the bug survived despite the board
having a dedicated placement-override fixture: under the old `!= 0` predicate both
endpoints behave identically to the fixed code, so the fixture passed before and after
the fix (verified by A/B, see below).

Pure-JUnit `FieldSpecKnownTest.everyProperSubsetOfKnownBitsIsNotKnown` now covers the
interior exhaustively at the PREDICATE level. What remains uncovered is whether the
analyzer ever CONSTRUCTS such a state in a real flow -- an E2E question.

## Measured finding: the serial-shift strategy cannot produce a partial bank field

Probed it (2026-08-16). Added a throwaway interleaved chain to make_prg_mmc1_override
that clobbers A mid-sequence, intending prg_bank knownMask = 0b00011:

    LDA #$01
    STA $E000 / LSR    ; serial write 1: bit 0 = 1 (known)
    STA $E000 / LSR    ; serial write 2: bit 1 = 0 (known)
    LDA $C400,X        ; opaque indexed load -> A unresolvable
    STA $E000 / LSR    ; write 3: bit 2 (unknown)
    STA $E000 / LSR    ; write 4: bit 3 (unknown)
    STA $E000          ; write 5: bit 4 (unknown) -> COMMIT
    JSR $8000

RESULT: the state collapses to FULLY UNKNOWN, not partial. At the three stores after the
clobber (c045/c049/c04d) the analyzer plants Warning bookmarks and emits NO bank comment
at the commit -- the same shape as the existing unresolvable case (criterion O2).
SerialShiftBankSwitchStrategy does not carry the two already-shifted known bits across an
accumulator clobber; it abandons the commit instead.

A/B CONFIRMED (the rebuild is the test, per the realrom-ab-needs-rebuild discipline):
reverted the predicate to pre-fix `!= 0` semantics, rebuilt, re-ran. Output at the probe
JSR was BYTE-IDENTICAL to the fixed build -- `c050 bank -> 5 [user override]`,
`REF c050 -> W8000_M3_B5::8000` -- i.e. indistinguishable from the fully-unknown control
at c01d. So the probe added no coverage and was reverted, not committed.

## What is actually open

1. Which strategy, if any, CAN produce a partially-known multi-bit bank field at a
   retarget site? Candidates worth checking: MMC3's select/data pair (r6/r7 are 6-bit and
   smb3's real dumps DO show partial forms like
   `r7=26? [known: r7.0=0,r7.1=1,...; assumed from initial: r6.0..r6.5]`), and the
   discrete/memory-latch strategies where a field is assembled from two separate stores.
   NOTE the smb3 evidence suggests MMC3 genuinely reaches partial states -- so an
   MMC3-based override fixture is the more promising route than MMC1 serial shift.
2. Once a strategy that produces the state is identified, add an override fixture on that
   board asserting the override FIRES on partial knowledge. That is the true E2E
   regression test for grm-v6o.
3. Separately: is SerialShiftBankSwitchStrategy's collapse-on-clobber the RIGHT call, or
   should it preserve the bits already shifted in? Preserving them would be strictly more
   information and would make partial states reachable on MMC1 too. Not obviously worth
   doing on its own -- filed here as an observation, not a recommendation.

title: Untrack tools/banktest/__pycache__ bytecode and gitignore it
description:
tools/banktest/__pycache__/mkemutest.cpython-313.pyc is TRACKED IN GIT. It is compiled Python
bytecode, regenerated whenever mknesbanktest.py imports mkemutest, so it shows up modified in
`git status` after any generator run and gets swept into unrelated commits by `git add -A`.

Noticed 2026-08-16 while integrating grm-432: the subagent's `git add -A` picked it up, and the
resulting binary hunk then broke `git apply` on the patch ("cannot apply binary patch ... without
full index line"), which cost a round trip to diagnose. It has no business in the tree -- it is a
per-interpreter-version artifact (the cpython-313 in the name), so it is also wrong for anyone on
a different Python.

FIX: `git rm --cached tools/banktest/__pycache__/mkemutest.cpython-313.pyc` and add
`__pycache__/` (and `*.pyc`) to .gitignore. Check whether any other __pycache__ entries are
tracked at the same time -- `git ls-files '*__pycache__*'` currently returns just this one.

Low priority, but it is pure noise that recurs on every generator change and it has already
caused one integration failure.
close_reason: Closed

comments.author: Chris Bongaarts
comments.text:
DONE 2026-08-16 (commit b117179). git rm --cached on the one tracked bytecode file, plus
__pycache__/ and *.pyc in .gitignore so it cannot recur for any future shared module.

CORRECTION TO THIS BEAD'S PREMISE: the description said mknesbanktest.py imports mkemutest. It
does NOT -- the importer is mkprgloadtest.py, which reuses mkemutest.build() at a different load
address (grm-w8a). Caught by testing rather than reading: deleting __pycache__ and running
mknesbanktest.py did NOT regenerate it, which is what prompted the grep. Running mkprgloadtest.py
does. The .gitignore comment records the corrected version.

That detail is the whole reason only ONE bytecode file was ever committed: CPython caches only
modules that are IMPORTED, and every other generator is invoked directly as a script.

Verified: with the cache deleted outright, mknesbanktest.py regenerates all 14 ROMs and
mkprgloadtest.py succeeds; the cache reappears on the import path and is ignored;
`git ls-files | grep -E '__pycache__|\.pyc$'` returns nothing. Full gate SUITE OK (check).

title: mknesbanktest _write_rom: derive the iNES PRG size from len(prg) instead of a units-ambiguous prg_banks
description:
Found 2026-08-15 while building the MMC2 fixture (grm-tas); it cost that task a truncated-load
debugging cycle. No existing bead tracks it.

THE TRAP. tools/banktest/mknesbanktest.py:2386

    def _write_rom(outdir, filename, prg, mapper=MAPPER, prg_banks=PRG_BANKS):
        header = make_ines_header(prg_banks, 0, mapper)

prg_banks goes straight into iNES header byte 4 (make_ines_header:2378), which is defined by the
format as the PRG-ROM size in 16 KiB UNITS. But this module names its per-board bank counts in
each BOARD'S OWN bank size, and those disagree:

    board      constant       bank size            passing the constant means
    UxROM      PRG_BANKS 4    PRG_BANK_SIZE 16K    64K   -- correct
    MMC1       MMC1_BANKS 8   PRG_BANK_SIZE 16K    128K  -- correct
    serial     SERIAL_BANKS 8 PRG_BANK_SIZE 16K    128K  -- correct
    MMC3       MMC3_BANKS 8   MMC3_BANK_SIZE 8K    128K  -- WRONG, the ROM is 64K
    MMC2       MMC2_BANKS 8   MMC2_BANK_SIZE 8K    128K  -- WRONG, the ROM is 64K

So `prg_banks=<BOARD>_BANKS` is the obvious call to write, is correct on three boards, and
silently declares DOUBLE the size on the two boards whose banks are 8 KiB. The failure is a
declared-size/actual-size mismatch: the loader believes there is twice as much PRG as the file
holds, and the load truncates. Nothing names the units at the call site.

HOW THE TWO 8K BOARDS COPE TODAY, and why it is not a fix: both nesmmc3test and nesmmc2test simply
DO NOT PASS the parameter and inherit the default PRG_BANKS=4, i.e. 4 x 16K = 64K, which happens
to equal their real 8 x 8K = 64K. That is a COINCIDENCE that holds only while those fixtures are
exactly 64 KiB. Resize either one and it breaks again, silently, in the same way. The MMC2 comment
at :2978 documents the coincidence rather than removing it.

*** THE FIX (user's, 2026-08-15): make it bank-size-aware rather than hardcoded. *** The header
field is FULLY DETERMINED by the payload -- there is no information in prg_banks that len(prg)
does not already carry. So derive it and let the parameter go:

    def _write_rom(outdir, filename, prg, mapper=MAPPER, prg_banks=None):
        if prg_banks is None:
            assert len(prg) % 0x4000 == 0, \
                "PRG payload %d is not a whole number of 16 KiB iNES units" % len(prg)
            prg_banks = len(prg) // 0x4000

That makes every existing caller correct by construction, deletes the units ambiguity, and turns
a silently-truncated load into an assertion at generation time.

KEEP THE PARAMETER AS AN EXPLICIT OVERRIDE (default None), do not delete it outright -- a fixture
that DELIBERATELY declares a wrong or unusual header is a thing we will want: grm-dfj needs the
NES 2.0 exponent PRG-size form (h[9] low nibble 0xF), and grm-abg wants crafted-malformed inputs
for loader degrade paths. An override that must be written on purpose is fine; a default that is
wrong by units is not.

WHILE IN THERE: consider whether the five <BOARD>_BANKS constants should be renamed to say their
unit (e.g. MMC2_BANKS_8K), or whether the per-board *_PRG_SIZE constants -- which already exist
and are unambiguous -- should be what fixtures pass around. The root cause is that "banks" means
two different things in one module.

ACCEPTANCE: _write_rom derives the header count from len(prg); no caller passes prg_banks except
a deliberate-malformation case (none today); the assertion fires on a non-multiple-of-16K payload;
full gate green with every NES golden byte-identical (this must be a no-op on all current
fixtures -- if any golden moves, a fixture's declared size was wrong and that is a separate
finding worth reporting rather than blessing).

SEE ALSO the bd memory fixture-dispatch-two-sided, which records this trap alongside the other
one found in the same task: a fixture name not registered in VerifyBankTest.java's dispatch chain
falls through to the C64 checkBanktest() default and prints nonsense criteria instead of failing.
close_reason: Closed

comments.author: Chris Bongaarts
comments.text:
FIXED 2026-08-15 (commit a8fcea9), exactly as prescribed: prg_banks defaults to None and is
derived as len(prg)//0x4000 behind an assertion that the payload is a whole number of 16 KiB
iNES units. Explicit override retained for fixtures that must declare a deliberately wrong or
unusual header. Five now-dead prg_banks= arguments removed (nesserialtest, nesmmc1test,
nesmmc1overridetest, neswrappertest, nesrelaytest -- all SERIAL_BANKS/MMC1_BANKS = 8 and
correct as passed); the MMC2 comment documenting the 64 KiB coincidence is gone, since the
derivation now makes the point at the definition instead.

BYTE-NEUTRAL, verified independently by the integrator as well as the implementer: all 14
generated ROMs diff identical before and after. That is the substantive finding -- it proves
MMC3 and MMC2 were already emitting the CORRECT 64 KiB header, because their coincidental
default (4 x 16K) equals their real size (8 x 8K). So this was a latent trap, not a live
defect, and no golden file was ever implicated. The landmine detonated only on resize.

PRG_BANKS survives as the legitimate UxROM board bank count (still used at 385/444/589/844/
916/2492/2571); only its role as _write_rom's default is gone. No call site passes the
parameter any more. Full gate SUITE OK (check).

title: NES board: MMC5 (mapper 5) descriptor -- four PRG modes and banked PRG-RAM
description:
USER RULING 2026-08-15: "we should absolutely do MMC5." This retires the open judgment call in
docs/human-research-todo.md section 3, which had listed MMC5 as the board with the most local
samples but questioned whether it was worth the effort. Answer: yes.

FILED SEPARATELY FROM grm-tas ON PURPOSE. grm-tas is mapper 9 (MMC2) -- a narrow board with one
switchable 8K window and three fixed banks, shipped because Punch-Out!! is in GME scope. MMC5 is
the opposite: the most capable mapper Nintendo shipped, and folding it into an MMC2 bead would
hide a large piece of work behind a small one.

WHY IT IS WORTH IT: 16 local sample ROMs, the largest single count in the corpus survey -- more
than MMC2 (7), 118 (5), FME-7 (4). So the payoff is real, not speculative.

SOURCE OF RECORD: the NESdev wiki -- https://www.nesdev.org/wiki/Mapper is the index (the
project owner's primary reference); the detail lives on the MMC5 page it links to. Section 3 of
docs/human-research-todo.md lists the fact sheet a descriptor needs: window layout and
granularity, register addresses plus any addr_mask/addr_match decode, bank-number bit layout,
power-on/reset state, whether PRG mode is switchable, and the write protocol.

WHAT MAKES THIS HARDER THAN EVERY BOARD SHIPPED SO FAR -- scope this before writing YAML:
  - PRG MODE is switchable across FOUR modes (one 32K / two 16K / 16K+8K / four 8K), so the
    window plan varies at runtime far more than MMC1's or MMC3's. Our engine already models
    mode-varying boards (see nes-mmc1.yaml / nes-mmc3.yaml and the modeField machinery in
    BoardBankAnalyzer), so check how far that stretches BEFORE assuming it covers four modes.
  - PRG-RAM is also BANKED, and the $8000-$DFFF bank registers select ROM or RAM via a high
    bit. A bank number that can mean two different memories is a genuinely new shape here.
  - It has ExRAM, split-screen, a multiplier, and vertical-split modes. Almost all of that is
    PPU-side and IRRELEVANT to PRG analysis -- but say so explicitly in the descriptor comments
    rather than leaving a reader wondering whether it was missed.

EXPECT A SCHEMA QUESTION. If the four-mode plan or the ROM/RAM bank-select bit cannot be
expressed in the current descriptor vocabulary, that is a DESIGN decision and must come back to
the user -- do not invent schema. That is the most likely reason this bead stalls, so surface it
early rather than after a half-written YAML.

SEQUENCING: let grm-tas (MMC2) land first. It establishes a fresh in-repo precedent for adding a
board end to end -- descriptor, synthetic fixture, registration, golden -- against the current
tree, and it is small enough to review quickly. Then do this one against that pattern.

ACCEPTANCE: machines/nes-mmc5.yaml shipped with ines_mappers [5]; a synthetic banktest fixture
exercising a PRG bank switch and, if expressible, a PRG mode change; full gate green with no
pre-existing golden moved; the derived fact sheet recorded as a comment on this bead.

title: Are grm-mej.2 increment 2's two new bank annotations correct? (megaman d571, wizwarr ffa6)
description:
FOUND 2026-08-10 while measuring grm-mej.2 increment 2's blast radius.

THE OBSERVATION. A full real-ROM run reports megaman FAIL with a single diff line:

  -REALROM count bankComments 156
  +REALROM count bankComments 157

with refs.intoOverlay 1704 and instrs.inOverlay 7429 BOTH on the golden side, and no sample.*
line moving.

IT IS NOT grm-g73 JITTER, on two independent grounds:
  1. It reproduces. Two runs from the grm-mej.2 working tree and one from a stashed clean HEAD
     all give 157; the working-tree and clean-HEAD dumps are BYTE-IDENTICAL to each other
     (compared with RealRomDump's SAMPLE temporarily raised so the comparison covers the full
     comment list, not the 25-entry window).
  2. grm-g73's own ten-import measurement (2026-08-10, commit e7aeba3) records bankComments and
     warnings as CONSTANT across all of megaman's flips -- only refs.intoOverlay and
     instrs.inOverlay move, in opposite directions. A bankComments delta is outside the measured
     jitter signature entirely.

So current HEAD deterministically produces one more bank comment on megaman than its golden
records, and the golden is stale on that line.

LIKELY CAUSE, NOT YET VERIFIED. megaman.dump was last blessed at 71959b1 (grm-hum). 09d9c97
(grm-k90, 'Let a mini-inline scan cross the wrapper-split join') re-blessed contra, lifeforce
and wizwarr -- and skipped megaman. That is exactly the pattern that left smb3's golden stale
(788f09b re-blessed seven rows and skipped it, per grm-bj6). grm-k90 widened what a mini-inline
scan can resolve, so one additional resolved switch site on megaman is precisely the shape of
change it would produce.

THE ONE COMMAND THAT SETTLES IT: run 'realrom-test.sh check --only megaman' at 09d9c97^ and at
09d9c97 and compare the bankComments line. If it moves there, this is grm-k90's and the golden
just needs blessing (with 'rm -rf build/realrom-cache' first -- see grm-g73's footgun note, and
note the 20% jitter rate means the bless itself can capture the minority overlay state).

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND ONE COUNT. Until this is resolved megaman FAILs for TWO unrelated reasons
at once, so the row cannot be read at a glance by anyone measuring a change's blast radius --
which is what this tier exists for. It also already cost one false-regression scare: the
guidance in realrom-test.sh said the two overlay counts were the only jitter lines and 'any
other line moving is real', which pointed straight at a regression that did not exist. That
guidance has been corrected in the same session (realrom-test.sh's header and the
realrom-expected-baseline-fails memory).

IF IT IS NOT grm-k90, the same A/B bisect over the commits between 71959b1 and HEAD finds the
one that is, and the extra comment should be inspected on its merits before blessing -- a new
bank annotation is a claim about a real cartridge, not a number to be rubber-stamped.
close_reason: Answered: both annotations are WRONG, one cause -- a write-through shadow read back after a bank switch that bypassed it (NMI restore stores). Fix on grm-p9y; the separately-excluded interrupt-entry seeding on grm-913. Full evidence in this bead's ANSWERED comment.

comments.author: Chris Bongaarts
comments.text:
REFRAMED 2026-08-10. THE ORIGINAL HYPOTHESIS IN THIS BEAD'S DESCRIPTION IS WRONG -- read this
comment instead of it.

This bead was filed as 'megaman's golden is stale on bankComments, most likely unblessed since
grm-k90 (09d9c97)'. That was based on an A/B that did not rebuild between its two sides, so both
sides analyzed with the same installed extension (realrom-test.sh does not build). Redone with a
rebuild at each point:

  megaman at a rebuilt ac77ee6^  -> PASS, bankComments 156, matches the golden exactly
  megaman at a rebuilt ac77ee6   -> bankComments 157, the new line being 'd571 bank -> 4 (bank=4)'

So the delta is grm-mej.2 increment 2's own doing, not a stale golden and not grm-k90's. The
golden is fine; the question is whether the NEW ANNOTATION IS RIGHT.

Increment 2 made a load of a derived bank MIRROR resolve from tracked bank state. Across all 31
real-ROM rows of both manifests it produced exactly two new confident claims, both on
memory-latch boards:

  megaman (UxROM)  d571  (no comment)                     -> 'bank -> 4 (bank=4)'
  wizwarr (AxROM)  ffa6  'Bank state becomes unknown here' -> 'bank -> 0 (bank=0)', warning gone

THE QUESTION, per site: what loads the value stored there, is that source address one the
derivation typed as a mirror, and does it hold the LIVE bank at that point -- or a saved/stale
one, which would make the annotation confidently wrong and would have REMOVED the warning that
previously flagged it. That is the failure mode this bead family rates worse than no answer at
all.

wizwarr ffa6 is the suspicious one. $C5 is that title's bank shadow, and the Rare code around it
uses the PHA / ... / PLA / STA $C5 / STA $8000 save-restore bracket quoted in
MemoryLatchBankSwitchStrategy's depositHelperArgument javadoc. A restore store puts the OLD bank
back, which is exactly what H2 rules must NOT resolve from in-state. If ffa6 is that restore,
then either the cell was typed WRITE_THROUGH when it should have been SAVE_SLOT, or the
save-slot typing guard did not fire on this shape.

megaman d571 is a plain new claim with no prior warning, so it is the easier of the two.

NEITHER GOLDEN MAY BE BLESSED until this is answered. Tracked as an open item in
docs/human-research-todo.md section 1. Note megaman independently carries grm-g73 jitter, so read
d571 itself rather than the count line.

ALSO SETTLED HERE, so nobody re-measures it: the later widening commit (d0e295d) and grm-mej.2
increment 3 move NOTHING on any row -- verified by rebuilt A/B across
megaman/smb3/wizwarr/cv2/tmnt/zelda/blmaster.

comments.author: Chris Bongaarts
comments.text:
ANSWERED 2026-08-10 by the user (disassembler pass), then confirmed byte-exact against the pinned
ROMs in the same session.

THE ANSWER: BOTH ANNOTATIONS ARE WRONG, AND THEY ARE ONE BUG, NOT TWO.

Both sites are the tail of an NMI handler restoring the interrupted bank. Both handlers switch
banks by writing the LATCH DIRECTLY, BYPASSING THE SHADOW CELL -- which is the entire point of the
idiom: it leaves the shadow holding the pre-interrupt bank so the restore is a bare
'LDA shadow / STA latch'.

megaman (UxROM, NMI vector $D4A8, so both addresses are inside the NMI handler):

  D54C: A9 04     LDA #$04
  D54E: 8D 04 C0  STA $C004    ; -> bank 4. Does NOT touch $42. ($C000 = 00 01 02 .. 07,
  D551: 20 00 90  JSR $9000    ;   the UNROM bus-conflict table, so $C004 reads back 04)
  D554..D56C                   ; loop, JSR $9003 -- NMI work, running in bank 4
  D56E: A5 42     LDA $42      ; shadow: still holds the INTERRUPTED bank
  D570: AA        TAX
  D571: 9D 00 C0  STA $C000,X  ; RESTORE          <-- claimed 'bank -> 4 (bank=4)'
  D574..D57F                   ; ... PLA / TAY / PLA -> RTI

wizwarr (AxROM, NMI vector $FF86):

  FF9A: A5 00     LDA $00
  FF9C: 29 18     AND #$18     ; masks the PRG bits away -> provably bank 0
  FF9E: 8D 00 80  STA $8000    ; -> bank 0. Does NOT store back to $00
  FFA1: 20 55 EE  JSR $EE55
  FFA4: A5 00     LDA $00      ; shadow: still holds the INTERRUPTED bank
  FFA6: 8D 00 80  STA $8000    ; RESTORE          <-- claimed 'bank -> 0 (bank=0)'
  FFA9: 68 AA 68 A8 68 40      ; PLA/TAX/PLA/TAY/PLA/RTI

The correct answer at both restore stores is UNKNOWN: an NMI fires from arbitrary mainline
context, so the bank it puts back is whatever was live when the interrupt hit.

ROOT CAUSE. MemoryLatchBankSwitchStrategy.mirroredByte (src/main/java/retromachines/
MemoryLatchBankSwitchStrategy.java:294-312) answers a WRITE_THROUGH mirror load from tracked
in-state with NO PROOF THE SHADOW IS STILL COHERENT WITH THE LIVE BANK. Between D54E and D571
(and FF9E and FFA6) the shadow and the live bank have deliberately diverged. The existing
precedence ladder in StoredValueScanner reasons carefully about the OPPOSITE window -- shadow
written before the commit, so the shadow LEADS in-state (cv2 c183/c185/c187), which is why
forwarding outranks the mirror -- but nothing models in-state LEADING the shadow.

THREE THINGS THIS RULES OUT, so nobody re-spends the tokens:

1. NOT A DERIVATION BUG. $42 and $00 really are WRITE_THROUGH. wizwarr's write-through pairs are
   plainly visible in FUN_ff69: 'FF74 STA $00 / FF76 STA $8000' and 'FF7D STA $00 / FF7F STA
   $8000'. BankMirrors.Discovery is right; the defect is in CONSUMPTION. Do not go re-tighten the
   typing rules or the SAVE_SLOT guard.

2. NOT THE INTERRUPT-ENTRY SEEDING. runDataflow does seed NMI/IRQ entries fullyKnown(initial_state)
   (BoardBankAnalyzer.java:643-651; initial_state is 0 on both nes-axrom.map and nes-uxrom.map),
   and that IS unsound in general -- but neither wrong claim comes from it. megaman's 4 comes from
   D54E; wizwarr's 0 comes from FF9E, which is itself a CORRECT annotation ('AND #$18' genuinely
   proves the PRG bits zero). Filed separately; do not conflate.

3. NOT THE $C5 / RARE 'PHA ... PLA' BRACKET this bead and the TODO item hypothesised. wizwarr's
   bank shadow is $00, NOT $C5 ($C5 is ironsword's), and no stack save-restore is involved at ffa6
   at all. The hypothesis was wrong about the cell, the title and the shape -- but it pointed at
   the right site for the right reason (a restore must not resolve from in-state).

NOTE THE HARD PART FOR ANY FIX: wizwarr's 'ff9e bank -> 0' is CORRECT and 'ffa6 bank -> 0' two
instructions later is WRONG -- same value, same handler, same cell. The distinction cannot be made
by looking at the value; it needs the coherence question.

SCORECARD, stated plainly: these two claims are increment 2's ENTIRE observable real-ROM output on
the WRITE_THROUGH half. That half is currently 0 for 2.

DISPOSITION: this bead is closed (question answered). The fix moves to its own bead, which carries
the do-not-bless injunction for both goldens.

title: banktest scripts should use a repo-local work dir, not /tmp
description:
tools/banktest/build-and-test.sh and realrom-test.sh create their work dirs with mktemp under
/tmp (e.g. /tmp/tmp.gzkbrxZlyJ), and print that path on failure for inspection ("work dir kept
for inspection"). That path is outside every configured agent working directory, so reading the
kept dump/log to diagnose a failure triggers a permission prompt every time.

Requested by the user 2026-08-09 while diagnosing grm-67g, where diagnosis required reading
<work>/nesmmc3test2.dump and .log repeatedly.

is the obvious candidate, alongside the existing build/ghidra-home and build/realrom-cache, both
of which are already per-worktree and gitignored. Keep an env override (TMPDIR is already
honoured by mktemp; an explicit GRM_BANKTEST_WORK would be clearer) and keep the
delete-on-success / keep-on-failure behaviour.

Check both scripts and any helper they share; also check whether the kept-dir message should
print a repo-relative path so it is clickable.
close_reason:
Shipped: one shared grm_work_dir() in tools/banktest/lib/common.sh, four call sites. Work dirs now
default to <repo>/build/banktest-work/<tag>.XXXXXXXX instead of $TMPDIR, so the dir a failing run

prompt. build/ was already gitignored and already holds the other per-worktree scratch
(ghidra-home, banktest-cache, realrom-cache), so this just puts a run's artifacts with the
worktree that produced them.

Call sites: run-banktest.sh:122, realrom-test.sh:424, measure-overlay-scale.sh:57, and
build-and-test.sh:246. That last one was NOT on the original list and is the one real bonus: its
unzip staging dir fed 'mv "$SRC_DIR" "$EXT_TARGET"' where EXT_TARGET lives under build/, so

Still one FRESH dir per run (mktemp -d with a template), so concurrent runs cannot collide and the

normalize_opts) are unaffected. New base override GRM_BANKTEST_WORK; the pre-existing
REALROM_WORK_DIR / MEASURE_WORK_DIR still name an exact dir and still take precedence. Both are
documented in the two script headers that list environment overrides.

VERIFIED: bash -n on all five files; forced a full extension reinstall (rm build/ghidra-home/
.install-stamp) and confirmed the extinstall staging path works and cleans up; success leaves
build/banktest-work empty; a failing run prints
  == work dir: D:/git/ghidra-retro-machines/build/banktest-work/realrom.0xbl4SdM ==
and the kept .diff reads with no prompt; full gate 'build-and-test.sh check' SUITE OK.

title: Suppress or prune overlay banks for PRG modes the ROM never uses
description:
IDEA from the user, 2026-08-09, filed while settling grm-67g. Unrelated to that bug; do not fold in.

Boards with a switchable PRG MODE (MMC3's $8000 bit 6, MMC1's control register) get overlay blocks
created for EVERY mode the descriptor models. A ROM that only ever runs one mode therefore carries a
full set of blocks and spaces for windows it never uses. smb3 is the worked example: $8000 bit 6 is
set at every observed write, so PRG mode 1 is the only live mode, yet the mode-0 window blocks exist
regardless. blocks.total 103 / blocks.overlay 95 on that title.

WHY IT IS NOT TRIVIALLY SAFE, and this is the user's own framing: in theory a ROM could switch PRG
mode from code that has not been disassembled yet, so 'no mode-0 write seen' is an absence-of-
evidence argument, not proof. Worse, suppression at CREATION time would have to happen during the
LOAD, before any analysis has run -- which is exactly when the evidence does not exist yet. The two
halves of the problem pull in opposite directions.

SHAPES WORTH CONSIDERING (none chosen):
  (a) Post-analysis PRUNE rather than load-time suppression: create everything, then offer to remove
      mode-N blocks that hold zero instructions AND zero inbound references AND for which no
      mode-selecting write with that value was ever resolved. Evidence-based, and reversible by
      re-running the loader.
  (b) A user-invoked SCRIPT rather than automatic behaviour -- the user notes it is easy enough to
      delete them by hand today, which puts the real value in convenience, not correctness. That
      argues for an explicit, undoable action over anything that runs silently.
  (c) A per-game descriptor HINT (grm-hb6 tier) declaring the live mode for a known title. Sidesteps
      the inference problem entirely by making it a recorded fact rather than a deduction.

(c) is the honest fit for the per-game tier and (b) is the cheapest useful thing; (a) is the one that
needs the most care about what counts as evidence. Not urgent -- this is tidiness, not correctness.

comments.author: Chris Bongaarts
comments.text:
LISTED IN docs/human-research-todo.md section 4 (decisions only you can make), 2026-08-16.

Not because it needs more analysis -- because the bead already concedes the value is CONVENIENCE,
NOT CORRECTNESS, and that judgment is what decides how much machinery the three filed shapes
((a) evidence-based prune / (b) user-invoked script / (c) per-game hint) are worth. An agent
picking one of the three would be making a product call, not a technical one. No agent work
should start here until a shape is chosen.

title: smb3: unexplained helper FUN_c542 with unrecovered args at 867b/ac6d (new since 788f09b)
description:
Found in the smb3 realrom diff while settling grm-bj6 / grm-67g, and deliberately NOT folded into
either -- the human trace of smb3's banking (ffc2/ffd1/ffbf plus the direct sites c5f5/c9f7)
accounts for every disassembled direct write to $8000 and does not mention c542 at all.

WHAT APPEARS (new since 788f09b, absent from the golden):
  sample.warn 867b [NesBankingAnalyzer] ... call to bank-switch helper FUN_c542 whose bank argument
                   could not be recovered at this call site
  sample.warn ac6d  (same, same helper)

TWO POSSIBILITIES, and they want different responses:
  (a) c542 is a REAL bank-switch helper the human trace did not reach -- e.g. RAM-resident, reached
      only from a switched window, or a wrapper the trace did not walk into. Then these warnings are

  (b) c542 is a FALSE helper admitted by 788f09b's wrapper pass, in which case it is collateral of

CHECK (b) FIRST, and check it AFTER grm-67g lands -- it is free at that point: re-run smb3 and see
whether 867b/ac6d survive. Only if they survive is a human look at c542 worth asking for.

comments.author: Chris Bongaarts
comments.text:
NOW THE SOLE BLOCKER OF SMB3'S GOLDEN, as of grm-67g increment 2 (2026-08-09).

grm-67g recovered ca23/ca2e and brought refs.intoOverlay, instrs.inOverlay and bankComments all
back to the golden's values. The ONLY line still differing is:

    -REALROM count warnings 50
    +REALROM count warnings 52

and the two extra warnings are this bead's, both FUN_c542:

    867b  call to bank-switch helper FUN_c542 whose bank argument could not be recovered
    ac6d  call to bank-switch helper FUN_c542 whose bank argument could not be recovered

PROVEN TO PREDATE grm-67g's fix, not caused by it. The identical realrom check was run twice on
2026-08-09, once against the PRE-change installed extension and once after: both show warnings
50 -> 52 with 867b present. Only the refs/instrs/bankComments/ca23/ca2e lines moved between the
two runs. So this is not collateral from the inbound-argument-cell rule -- it is the same
unexplained regression this bead was filed for.

CONSEQUENCE FOR THE TRACKER: smb3 realrom cannot go green, and grm-bj6 cannot close, until this is
